#uuid "63775110-b76b-5425-a979-1d472435c3ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-107114" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $A=\{\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & 1\end{bmatrix}\,|\,a,b,c\in R\}.$ Which of the following statements are true? I. $A$ is closed under matrix addition II. $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication III. $A$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ IV. $A$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication. With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. - Statement I is false. If ${A}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} & {b}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and ${A}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{2} & {b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & 1\end{bmatrix}$ are two matrices from $A,$ then $$ \begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} & {b}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{2} & {b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+{a}_{2} & {b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}+{c}_{2} & 2\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned} $$ which is not a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is *not* closed under addition. - Statement II is false. If $A=\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & 1\end{bmatrix}$ is an element of $A,$ then $$ \begin{aligned}2A & =k\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2a & 2b \\ 2c & 2\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned} $$ which is not a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication. - Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $A$ is a *not* subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a4c1e3e7-b7eb-5780-ac9f-e4101be00453"] :db/ensure "Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,2]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=4{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+xy-3{y}^{2}-2. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[1,\,2]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**
${x}_{1}≈[$ {{field-1}} $]$
{{field-2}}
" :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is $$ {x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}), $$ where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$ In our case, the gradient is $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+xy-3{y}^{2}-2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+xy-3{y}^{2}-2)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}8xy-4x+y \\ 4{x}^{2}+x-6y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned} $$ and the Hessian is $$ \begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(8xy-4x+y) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}+x-6y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(8xy-4x+y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}+x-6y)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}8y-4 & 8x+1 \\ 8x+1 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is $$ {x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}8y-4 & 8x+1 \\ 8x+1 & -6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}8xy-4x+y \\ 4{x}^{2}+x-6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}. $$ Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}8y-4 & 8x+1 \\ 8x+1 & -6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}8xy-4x+y \\ 4{x}^{2}+x-6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}8(2)-4 & 8(1)+1 \\ 8(1)+1 & -6\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}8(1)(2)-4(1)+2 \\ 4(1)^{2}+(1)-6(2)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}12 & 9 \\ 9 & -6\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}14 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{12\cdot (-6)-9\cdot 9}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -9 \\ -9 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}14 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{153}\begin{bmatrix}-21 \\ -210\end{bmatrix} \\ & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.863 \\ 0.627\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9722e690-313b-51ec-99a5-45188eea87c3" :question/problem "Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "A $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+xy+2x+y)\text{ }j \\ & =(2x+y+2)\text{ }i+(-2y+x+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(1,-1) & :answer/value "j+4\,k" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125740 :tutorial/content "The same property holds true in the case of three or more variables. In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if the gradient vector is nonzero, i.e., $$ \nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0, $$ then we have the following result: *$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$* To illustrate, let's consider the function $$ w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right). $$ The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$ The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned} \nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \\[5pt] &= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\\[5pt] &= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\\[10pt] \nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle. \end{aligned} $$ Now clearly, $\nabla f (0,0, 1)$ is perpendicular to $\mathcal S$ at the point $(0,0,1).$ ![](images/88/88bf25de31ae3318379865cdf2590c15216cb984cbf3948f975caa47317be664.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203943 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45" :question/id #uuid "e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45" :question/math-academy-id "q-225260" :question/problem "**Fully** factor the following trinomial. $-12{a}^{2}-6a+6=$ {{field-1}}$(a\,+$ {{field-2}} $)($ {{field-3}} $a\,-1)$" :question/worked-solution "We need to factor the following expression: $$ -12{a}^{2}-6a+6 $$ First, notice that all the terms have a common factor of $-6.$ So, we can simplify the calculation by first factoring out $-6:$ $$ \begin{aligned}-6(2{a}^{2}+a-1)\end{aligned} $$ Now, we just need to factor the trinomial $2{a}^{2}+a-1$ in parentheses. To do this, we find two numbers that - multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant (which is $2\times (-1)=-2$), and - add to the linear coefficient (which is $1$). The factor pairs of $-2$ are $$ (1,-2),\,(-1,2). $$ Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-1,2)$ add to $1:$ $$ -1+2=1\,✓ $$ Then, we write the linear term as $-a+2a,$ and factor the result by grouping: $$ \begin{aligned}2{a}^{2}+a-1 & = \\ 2{a}^{2}-a+2a-1 & = \\ (2{a}^{2}-a)+(2a-1) & = \\ a(2a-1)+(2a-1) & = \\ (a+1)(2a-1) & \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the original trinomial factors as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}-12{a}^{2}-6a+6 & = \\ -6(2{a}^{2}+a-1) & = \\ -6(a+1)(2a-1) & \end{aligned} $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields "7002a70c-d40e-53ed-9d27-c94492760a6a" :question/math-academy-id "q-22036" :question/problem "![](images/a3/a36fe195458e459aea993232a72ed21e0c780135dc4dbe4bece45bfc3b6e50e2.png) The perimeter of the above triangle is $50+25\sqrt{2}.$ Find the measure of each leg." :question/worked-solution "Because the triangle is isosceles, the legs must have the same length. Let $a$ be the length of each leg. So, we have $$ AB=BC=a. $$ Moreover, because the triangle is a *right* isosceles triangle, the hypotenuse must be equal to $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg. Therefore, $$ AC=AB\cdot \sqrt{2}=a\sqrt{2}. $$ Finally, since the perimeter is $p=50+25\sqrt{2},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+AC \\ 50+25\sqrt{2} & =a+a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 25(2+\sqrt{2}) & =2a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 25(2+\sqrt{2}) & =(2+\sqrt{2})a \\ 25\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})} & =\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})}a \\ 25 & =a\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the measure of a leg is $25.$" :question/difficulty #uuid "7f25e8cf-a84e-5491-8095-e34846bd72c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-109613" :question/problem "Write $y=\frac{1}{5}x+2$ in standard form." :question/worked-solution "Our goal is to write the equation in the form $ax+by=c,$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors and $a\ge 0.$ We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side. This gives $$ -\frac{1}{5}x+y=2 $$ Now, we multiply both sides of the equation by $-1:$ $$ \begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}x+y & =2 \\ (-1)\cdot (-\frac{1}{5}x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (2) \\ \frac{1}{5}x-y & =-2.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we multiply both sides of the equation by $5:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}x-y & =-2 \\ 5\cdot (\frac{1}{5}x-y) & =5\cdot (-2) \\ x-5y & =-10.\end{aligned} $$ Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So we are done! The standard form of the line is $x-5y=-10.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dad8335d-f4a7-566b-a578-6ac7a63c8d7b"] :db/ensure First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function $$ y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=2x. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2. $$ We now apply the chain rule, and get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\ & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\cdot (2) \\ & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).\end{aligned} $$ Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{8},$ we find $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\ & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ & =\sqrt{2}\,.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ is $\sqrt{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cd275e51-d3ee-5c23-a80e-981590060edc"] following predicate: $\,$ $a+b$ is an odd number, where the universal set is $\{(a,b)\,|\,a=2,3,\,b=5,8\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The *truth set* of a predicate $P({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})$ is the set of $n$-tuples in its universal set $U={U}_{1}\times {U}_{2}\times ⋯\times {U}_{n}$ such that substituting these tuples for the variables makes the predicate a true statement: $$ T=\{({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\in U\,|\,P({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\} $$ The universal set for our predicate is $$ \begin{aligned}U & =\{2,3\}\times \{5,8\} \\ & =\{(2,5),(2,8),(3,5),(3,8)\}.\end{aligned} $$ We need to find $(a,b)\in U$ such that the following is true: $\,$ $a+b$ is an odd number The following pairs give the elements of our truth set: - $(2,5)$ since $2+5=7$ and $7$ is an odd number, - $(3,8)$ since $3+8=11$ and $11$ is an odd number. Therefore, the truth set of our predicate is $$ T=\{(2,5),(3,8)\}. $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-28f10fe3-37fc-540c-8f33-9718dc4bbd85"] :question/id #uuid "f74663e2-eda6-5c43-8b1e-ec79f6eff3d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-129445" :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2$ at the point $(1,2,2).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as $$ z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}). $$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2) \\ & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2) \\ & =2{x}^{3}y\end{aligned} $$ Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(1,2):$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2) & =3({1}^{2})({2}^{2})=12 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) & =2({1}^{3})(2)=4\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane: $$ \begin{aligned}z-2 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) \\ z-2 & =12(x-1)+4(y-2) \\ z-2 & =12x+4y-20 \\ 12x+4y-z-18 & =0\end{aligned} $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,0,2,5).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as $$ w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}). $$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=-2y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2z\end{aligned} $$ Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,0,2):$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,2) & =2(1)=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,2) & =-2(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,2) & =2(2)=4\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane: $$ \begin{aligned}w-5 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,2)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,2)+(z-2)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,2) \\ w-5 & =2(x-1)+0y+4(z-2) \\ w-5 & =2x+4z-10 \\ 2x+4z-w-5 & =0\end{aligned} $$" :question/difficulty at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $$ f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a). $$ Notice that the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem. Substituting $a=⟨-1,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,-2⟩$ into the above expression, we get $$ \begin{aligned}f(2,-2)-f(-1,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,-2⟩-⟨-1,1⟩) \\ ((-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+1)-({1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 9-3 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 6 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,2y⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},2{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}6 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 6 & =⟨2{c}_{1},2{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 6 & =6{c}_{1}-6{c}_{2} \\ 1 & ={c}_{1}-{c}_{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line. $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{-2-1} & =\frac{x-(-1)}{2-(-1)} \\ \frac{y-1}{(-3)} & =\frac{x+1}{3} \\ y-1 & =-(x+1) \\ y & =-x.\end{aligned} $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =-{c}_{1}.\end{aligned} $$ Substituting the above into the equation ${c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=1,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-(-{c}_{1}) & =1 \\ 2{c}_{1} & =1 \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we find ${c}_{2}=-{c}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$" :question/difficulty $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem. Substituting $a=⟨-2,-8⟩$ and $b=⟨1,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get $$ \begin{aligned}f(1,0)-f(-2,-8) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,0⟩-⟨-2,-8⟩) \\ (0-{1}^{3})-(-8-(-2)^{3}) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,8⟩ \\ -1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,8⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-3{x}^{2},1⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-3{c}_{1}^{2},1⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}-1 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨3,8⟩ \\ -1 & =⟨-3{c}_{1}^{2},1⟩\cdot ⟨3,8⟩ \\ -1 & =-9{c}_{1}^{2}+8 \\ 9{c}_{1}^{2} & =9 \\ {c}_{1}^{2} & =1 \\ {c}_{1} & =\pm 1.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line. $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-(-8)}{0-(-8)} & =\frac{x-(-2)}{1-(-2)} \\ \frac{y+8}{8} & =\frac{x+2}{3} \\ y+8 & =\frac{8(x+2)}{3} \\ y & =\frac{8(x-1)}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{8({c}_{1}-1)}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem. - For ${c}_{1}=-1,$ we obtain $$ {c}_{2}=\frac{8(-1-1)}{3}=-\frac{16}{3}. $$ Therefore, the coordinates of the first point are $(-1,-\frac{16}{3}).$ - For ${c}_{1}=1,$ we obtain $$ {c}_{2}=\frac{8(1-1)}{3}=0. $$ Therefore, the "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $$ f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a). $$ Notice that $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{3}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem. Substituting $a=⟨0,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,-1,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get $$ \begin{aligned}f(1,-1,0)-f(0,0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,-1,0⟩-⟨0,0,1⟩) \\ 1-(-1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 2 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨0,2y,-3{z}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨0,2{c}_{2},-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we get $$ \begin{aligned}2 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 2 & =⟨0,2{c}_{2},-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 2 & =-2{c}_{2}+3{c}_{3}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line. $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{(-1)}=\frac{z-1}{(-1)} \\ x & =-y=1-z\end{aligned} $$ Parametrizing the line, we get $$ x=t\,\,y=-t,\,z=1-t,\,0\le t\le 1. $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ {c}_{1}=t\,\,{c}_{2}=-t,\,{c}_{3}=1-t. $$ Substituting the above in the equation $-2{c}_{2}+3{c}_{3}^{2}=2,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}-2(-t)+3(1-t)^{2} & =2 \\ 2t+3{t}^{2}-6t+3 & =2 \\ 3{t}^{2}-4t+1 & =0 \\ (3t-1)(t-1) & =0 \\ t & =\frac{1}{3},\,1.\end{aligned} $$ Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem. - For $t=\frac{1}{3},$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}, \\ {c}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{3}, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, the coordinates of the first point $C$ are $(\frac{1}{3},-\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}).$ - For $t=1,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =1, \\ {c}_{2} & =-1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-1=0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, the coordinates of the second point $C$ are $(1,-1,0).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields :question/problem "Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨-2,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨0,-2,0⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $$ f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a). $$ Notice that $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem. Substituting $a=⟨-2,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨0,-2,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get $$ \begin{aligned}f(0,-2,0)-f(-2,0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨0,-2,0⟩-⟨-2,0,1⟩) \\ -4-1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩ \\ -5 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨0,-2y,2z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨0,-2{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we get $$ \begin{aligned}-5 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩ \\ -5 & =⟨0,-2{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩ \\ -5 & =4{c}_{2}-2{c}_{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line. $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x-(-2)}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{(-2)}=\frac{z-1}{(-1)} \\ \frac{x+2}{2} & =-\frac{y}{2}=1-z\end{aligned} $$ Parametrizing the line, we get $$ x=2t-2,\,y=-2t,\,z=1-t,\,0\le t\le 1. $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ {c}_{1}=2t-2,\,{c}_{2}=-2t,\,{c}_{3}=1-t. $$ Substituting the above in the equation $4{c}_{2}-2{c}_{3}=-5,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}4(-2t)-2(1-t) & =-5 \\ -8t-2+2t & =-5 \\ -6t & =-3 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =2(\frac{1}{2})-2=-1, \\ {c}_{2} & =-2(\frac{1}{2})=-1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(-1,-1,\frac{1}{2}).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1589433d-cfd2-5a34-998a-3aeb17064001"] :db/ensure \operatorname{csc}⁡x(6\operatorname{csc}⁡x-5\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int (6{csc}^{2}⁡x-5\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\text{d}x \\ & =\int 6{csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x-\int =6(-\operatorname{cot}⁡x)-5(-\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+C \\ & =-6\operatorname{cot}⁡x+5\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned} $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :tutorial/content "We know that the derivative of sine is cosine: $$ \dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\sin{x}) = \cos{x} $$ Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we see that the integral of cosine is sine: $$ \int \cos{x}\,\textrm d x = \sin{x} + C $$ We can discover two other integrals by considering the derivatives of cosine and tangent: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned} $$ Similarly, by considering the derivatives of secant, cosecant, and cotangent, we arrive at $$ \begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C \\ \int \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C \\ \int {csc}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C.\end{aligned} $$ With these six formulas, we can integrate many different trigonometric functions." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064392 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186233095 "Here, we apply the addition, constant multiple, and power rules: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{4}+\frac{4}{{x}^{3}}+12) \\ & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{4})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{-3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12) \\ & =3\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4})+4\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{-3})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12) \\ & =3\cdot 4{x}^{(4-1)}+4\cdot (-3){x}^{(-3-1)}+0 \\ & =12{x}^{3}-12{x}^{-4} \\ & =12{x}^{3}-\frac{12}{{x}^{4}}\end{aligned} $$" \begin{aligned}{b}_{1}\cdot {b}_{1} & ={b}_{1}^{2}+{b}_{2}^{2} \\ & ={2}^{2}+(-3)^{2} \\ & =4+9 \\ & =13 \\ {b}_{1}\cdot a & ={b}_{1}{a}_{1}+{b}_{2}{a}_{2} \\ & =2\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot (-1) \\ & =4+3 \\ & If ${A}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} & {b}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and ${A}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{2} & {b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & 1\end{bmatrix}$ are two matrices from $A,$ then $$ \begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} & {b}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{2} & {b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+{a}_{2} & {b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}+{c}_{2} & 2\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned} $$ which is not a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is *not* closed under addition. - Statement II is false. If $A=\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & 1\end{bmatrix}$ is an element of $A,$ then $$ \begin{aligned}2A & =k\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2a & 2b \\ 2c & 2\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned} $$ which is not a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication. - Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $A$ is a *not* subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication. "Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,2]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=4{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+xy-3{y}^{2}-2. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[1,\,2]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**
${x}_{1}≈[$ {{field-1}} $]$
{{field-2}}
" :question/worked-solution "The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is $$ {x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}), $$ where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$ In our case, the gradient is $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+xy-3{y}^{2}-2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+xy-3{y}^{2}-2)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}8xy-4x+y \\ 4{x}^{2}+x-6y\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned} $$ and the Hessian is $$ \begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂}{∂x}(8xy-4x+y) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}+x-6y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(8xy-4x+y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}+x-6y)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}8y-4 & 8x+1 \\ 8x+1 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is $$ {x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{\begin{bmatrix}8y-4 & 8x+1 \\ 8x+1 & -6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}8xy-4x+y \\ 4{x}^{2}+x-6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{n}}. $$ Starting with ${x}_{0}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{\begin{bmatrix}8y-4 & 8x+1 \\ 8x+1 & -6\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{\begin{bmatrix}8xy-4x+y \\ 4{x}^{2}+x-6y\end{bmatrix}}_{{x}_{0}} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}8(2)-4 & 8(1)+1 \\ 8(1)+1 & -6\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}8(1)(2)-4(1)+2 \\ 4(1)^{2}+(1)-6(2)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-{\begin{bmatrix}12 & 9 \\ 9 & -6\end{bmatrix}}^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}14 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\frac{1}{12\cdot (-6)-9\cdot 9}\begin{bmatrix}-6 & -9 \\ -9 & 12\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}14 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{153}\begin{bmatrix}-21 \\ -210\end{bmatrix} \\ & ≈\begin{bmatrix}0.863 \\ 0.627\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9722e690-313b-51ec-99a5-45188eea87c3" :answer/value "j+4\,k" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125740 :tutorial/content "The same property holds true in the case of three or more variables. In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if the gradient vector is nonzero, i.e., $$ \nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0, $$ then we have the following result: *$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$* To illustrate, let's consider the function $$ w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right). $$ The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$ The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned} \nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \\[5pt] &= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\\[5pt] &= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\\[10pt] \nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle. \end{aligned} $$ Now clearly, $\nabla f (0,0, 1)$ is perpendicular to $\mathcal S$ at the point $(0,0,1).$ ![](images/88/88bf25de31ae3318379865cdf2590c15216cb984cbf3948f975caa47317be664.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203943 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45" :question/id #uuid "e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45" :question/math-academy-id "q-225260" :question/problem "**Fully** factor the following trinomial. $-12{a}^{2}-6a+6=$ {{field-1}}$(a\,+$ {{field-2}} $)($ {{field-3}} $a\,-1)$" :question/worked-solution "We need to factor the following expression: $$ -12{a}^{2}-6a+6 $$ First, notice that all the terms have a common factor of $-6.$ So, we can simplify the calculation by first factoring out $-6:$ $$ \begin{aligned}-6(2{a}^{2}+a-1)\end{aligned} $$ Now, we just need to factor the trinomial $2{a}^{2}+a-1$ in parentheses. To do this, we find two numbers that - multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant (which is $2\times (-1)=-2$), and - add to the linear coefficient (which is $1$). The factor pairs of $-2$ are $$ (1,-2),\,(-1,2). $$ Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-1,2)$ add to $1:$ $$ -1+2=1\,✓ $$ Then, we write the linear term as $-a+2a,$ and factor the result by grouping: $$ \begin{aligned}2{a}^{2}+a-1 & = \\ 2{a}^{2}-a+2a-1 & = \\ (2{a}^{2}-a)+(2a-1) & = \\ a(2a-1)+(2a-1) & = \\ (a+1)(2a-1) & \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the original trinomial factors as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}-12{a}^{2}-6a+6 & = \\ -6(2{a}^{2}+a-1) & = \\ -6(a+1)(2a-1) & \end{aligned} $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields above triangle is $50+25\sqrt{2}.$ Find the measure of each leg." :question/worked-solution "Because the triangle is isosceles, the legs must have the same length. Let $a$ be the length of each leg. So, we have $$ AB=BC=a. $$ Moreover, because the triangle is a *right* isosceles triangle, the hypotenuse must be equal to $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg. Therefore, $$ AC=AB\cdot \sqrt{2}=a\sqrt{2}. $$ Finally, since the perimeter is $p=50+25\sqrt{2},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+AC \\ 50+25\sqrt{2} & =a+a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 25(2+\sqrt{2}) & =2a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 25(2+\sqrt{2}) & =(2+\sqrt{2})a \\ 25\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})} & =\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})}a \\ 25 & =a\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the measure of a leg is $25.$" :question/difficulty #uuid "7f25e8cf-a84e-5491-8095-e34846bd72c0" :question/math-academy-id "q-109613" :question/problem "Write $y=\frac{1}{5}x+2$ in standard form." :question/worked-solution "Our goal is to write the equation in the form $ax+by=c,$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors and $a\ge 0.$ We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side. This gives $$ -\frac{1}{5}x+y=2 $$ Now, we multiply both sides of the equation by $-1:$ $$ \begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}x+y & =2 \\ (-1)\cdot (-\frac{1}{5}x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (2) \\ \frac{1}{5}x-y & =-2.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we multiply both sides of the equation by $5:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}x-y & =-2 \\ 5\cdot (\frac{1}{5}x-y) & =5\cdot (-2) \\ x-5y & =-10.\end{aligned} $$ Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So we are done! The standard form of the line is $x-5y=-10.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dad8335d-f4a7-566b-a578-6ac7a63c8d7b"] :db/ensure predicate a true statement: $$ T=\{x\in U\,|\,P(x)\} $$ The universal set for our predicate is $U=R.$ We need to find $x\in U$ such that the following is true: $\,$ ${x}^{2}-8=2x$ Now, we solve the above equation by factoring: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-8 & =2x \\ {x}^{2}-2x-8 & =0 \\ (x-4)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned} $$ So, the solutions are $x=-2\in R$ and $x=4\in R.$ Therefore, the truth set of our following predicate: $\,$ $a+b$ is an odd number, where the universal set is $\{(a,b)\,|\,a=2,3,\,b=5,8\}.$" :question/worked-solution "The *truth set* of a predicate $P({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})$ is the set of $n$-tuples in its universal set $U={U}_{1}\times {U}_{2}\times ⋯\times {U}_{n}$ such that substituting these tuples for the variables makes the predicate a true statement: $$ T=\{({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\in U\,|\,P({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\} $$ The universal set for our predicate is $$ \begin{aligned}U & =\{2,3\}\times \{5,8\} \\ & =\{(2,5),(2,8),(3,5),(3,8)\}.\end{aligned} $$ We need to find $(a,b)\in U$ such that the following is true: $\,$ $a+b$ is an odd number The following pairs give the elements of our truth set: - $(2,5)$ since $2+5=7$ and $7$ is an odd number, - $(3,8)$ since $3+8=11$ and $11$ is an odd number. Therefore, the truth set of our predicate is $$ T=\{(2,5),(3,8)\}. $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-28f10fe3-37fc-540c-8f33-9718dc4bbd85"] :question/id #uuid "f74663e2-eda6-5c43-8b1e-ec79f6eff3d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-129445" :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2$ at the point $(1,2,2).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as $$ z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}). $$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2) \\ & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2) \\ & =2{x}^{3}y\end{aligned} $$ Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(1,2):$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2) & =3({1}^{2})({2}^{2})=12 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) & =2({1}^{3})(2)=4\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane: $$ \begin{aligned}z-2 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) \\ z-2 & =12(x-1)+4(y-2) \\ z-2 & =12x+4y-20 \\ 12x+4y-z-18 & =0\end{aligned} $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as $$ w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}). $$ First, we find the partial derivatives: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=-2y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})=2z\end{aligned} $$ Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,0,2):$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,2) & =2(1)=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,2) & =-2(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,2) & =2(2)=4\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane: $$ \begin{aligned}w-5 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,2)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,2)+(z-2)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,2) \\ w-5 & =2(x-1)+0y+4(z-2) \\ w-5 & =2x+4z-10 \\ 2x+4z-w-5 & =0\end{aligned} $$" :question/difficulty So, we have $$ \lim_{x\to \infty}\sqrt{x} = \infty. $$ On the other hand, when computing the limit as $x \to -\infty,$ remember that the square root function isn't defined for $x<0.$ Therefore, $$ \lim_{x\to -\infty}\sqrt{x} = \textrm{DNE}. $$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130326 :tutorial/content "Consider the graph of the cube root function $y=\sqrt[3]{x}$ below. the limit of the cube root function can be obtained by simply substituting $x=a$ into the cube root: $$ \lim_{x\to a} \sqrt[3]{x} = \sqrt[3]{a} $$ Additionally, we can see from the graph that the limits at infinity are $$ \lim_{x\to \infty} \sqrt[3]{x} = \infty \qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_{x\to -\infty} \sqrt[3]{x} = -\infty. $$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129334 "551372ab-8536-5d27-a0f1-42bcde72d2ee" :question/math-academy-id "q-106067" :question/problem "Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨-1,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,-2⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $$ f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a). $$ Notice that the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem. Substituting $a=⟨-1,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,-2⟩$ into the above expression, we get $$ \begin{aligned}f(2,-2)-f(-1,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,-2⟩-⟨-1,1⟩) \\ ((-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+1)-({1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 9-3 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 6 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,2y⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},2{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}6 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 6 & =⟨2{c}_{1},2{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨3,-3⟩ \\ 6 & =6{c}_{1}-6{c}_{2} \\ 1 & ={c}_{1}-{c}_{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line. $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{-2-1} & =\frac{x-(-1)}{2-(-1)} \\ \frac{y-1}{(-3)} & =\frac{x+1}{3} \\ y-1 & =-(x+1) \\ y & =-x.\end{aligned} $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =-{c}_{1}.\end{aligned} $$ Substituting the above into the equation ${c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=1,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-(-{c}_{1}) & =1 \\ 2{c}_{1} & =1 \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we find ${c}_{2}=-{c}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$" :question/difficulty =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,8⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-3{x}^{2},1⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-3{c}_{1}^{2},1⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}-1 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨3,8⟩ \\ -1 & =⟨-3{c}_{1}^{2},1⟩\cdot ⟨3,8⟩ \\ -1 & =-9{c}_{1}^{2}+8 \\ 9{c}_{1}^{2} & =9 \\ {c}_{1}^{2} & =1 \\ {c}_{1} & =\pm 1.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line. $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-(-8)}{0-(-8)} & =\frac{x-(-2)}{1-(-2)} \\ \frac{y+8}{8} & =\frac{x+2}{3} \\ y+8 & =\frac{8(x+2)}{3} \\ y & =\frac{8(x-1)}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{8({c}_{1}-1)}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem. - For ${c}_{1}=-1,$ we obtain $$ {c}_{2}=\frac{8(-1-1)}{3}=-\frac{16}{3}. $$ Therefore, the coordinates of the first point are $(-1,-\frac{16}{3}).$ - For ${c}_{1}=1,$ we obtain $$ {c}_{2}=\frac{8(1-1)}{3}=0. $$ Therefore, the value theorem for $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{3}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,-1,0⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $$ f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a). $$ Notice that $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{3}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem. Substituting $a=⟨0,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,-1,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get $$ \begin{aligned}f(1,-1,0)-f(0,0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,-1,0⟩-⟨0,0,1⟩) \\ 1-(-1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 2 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨0,2y,-3{z}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨0,2{c}_{2},-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we get $$ \begin{aligned}2 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 2 & =⟨0,2{c}_{2},-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 2 & =-2{c}_{2}+3{c}_{3}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line. $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{(-1)}=\frac{z-1}{(-1)} \\ x & =-y=1-z\end{aligned} $$ Parametrizing the line, we get $$ x=t\,\,y=-t,\,z=1-t,\,0\le t\le 1. $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ {c}_{1}=t\,\,{c}_{2}=-t,\,{c}_{3}=1-t. $$ Substituting the above in the equation $-2{c}_{2}+3{c}_{3}^{2}=2,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}-2(-t)+3(1-t)^{2} & =2 \\ 2t+3{t}^{2}-6t+3 & =2 \\ 3{t}^{2}-4t+1 & =0 \\ (3t-1)(t-1) & =0 \\ t & =\frac{1}{3},\,1.\end{aligned} $$ Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem. - For $t=\frac{1}{3},$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}, \\ {c}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{3}, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, the coordinates of the first point $C$ are $(\frac{1}{3},-\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}).$ - For $t=1,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =1, \\ {c}_{2} & =-1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-1=0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, the coordinates of the second point $C$ are $(1,-1,0).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $$ f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a). $$ Notice that $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem. Substituting $a=⟨-2,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨0,-2,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get $$ \begin{aligned}f(0,-2,0)-f(-2,0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨0,-2,0⟩-⟨-2,0,1⟩) \\ -4-1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩ \\ -5 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨0,-2y,2z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨0,-2{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we get $$ \begin{aligned}-5 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩ \\ -5 & =⟨0,-2{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩ \\ -5 & =4{c}_{2}-2{c}_{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line. $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x-(-2)}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{(-2)}=\frac{z-1}{(-1)} \\ \frac{x+2}{2} & =-\frac{y}{2}=1-z\end{aligned} $$ Parametrizing the line, we get $$ x=2t-2,\,y=-2t,\,z=1-t,\,0\le t\le 1. $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ {c}_{1}=2t-2,\,{c}_{2}=-2t,\,{c}_{3}=1-t. $$ Substituting the above in the equation $4{c}_{2}-2{c}_{3}=-5,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}4(-2t)-2(1-t) & =-5 \\ -8t-2+2t & =-5 \\ -6t & =-3 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =2(\frac{1}{2})-2=-1, \\ {c}_{2} & =-2(\frac{1}{2})=-1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(-1,-1,\frac{1}{2}).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1589433d-cfd2-5a34-998a-3aeb17064001"] :db/ensure of cosine is sine: $$ \int \cos{x}\,\textrm d x = \sin{x} + C $$ We can discover two other integrals by considering the derivatives of cosine and tangent: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned} $$ Similarly, by considering the derivatives of secant, cosecant, and cotangent, we arrive at $$ \begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C \\ \int \operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{cot}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C \\ \int {csc}^{2}⁡x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cot}⁡x+C.\end{aligned} $$ With these six formulas, we can integrate many different trigonometric functions." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064392 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186233095 To quickly compute the numerator $3u\cdot v,$ we multiply $u\cdot v$ by $3.$ Doing this, we get $$ \begin{aligned}(3u)\cdot v & =3(u\cdot v) \\ & =3\cdot 22 \\ & =66.\end{aligned} $$ To quickly =2({u}_{1}^{2}+{u}_{2}^{2}+{u}_{3}^{2}+{u}_{4}^{2}) \\ & =2({2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{5}^{2}) \\ & =2(4+1+9+25) \\ & =2\cdot 39 \\ & =78.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \frac{(3u)\cdot v}{u\cdot (2u)}=\frac{66}{78}=\frac{11}{13}. $$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5bf3387a-a036-5d98-81f1-318396ac1845"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} ["question-63775110-b76b-5425-a979-1d472435c3ac" :question/problem "Consider the vector space ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ of all $2\times 2$ matrices over $R$ and its subset $A=\{\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & 1\end{bmatrix}\,|\,a,b,c\in R\}.$ Which of the following statements are true? I. $A$ is closed under matrix addition II. $A$ is closed under scalar multiplication III. $A$ is a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$ IV. $A$ is **not** a subspace of ${\text{M}}_{2}(R)$"] ["question-63775110-b76b-5425-a979-1d472435c3ac" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a subset of a vector space is a subspace if it's closed under addition and scalar multiplication. With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. - Statement I is false. If ${A}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} & {b}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and ${A}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{2} & {b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & 1\end{bmatrix}$ are two matrices from $A,$ then $$ \begin{aligned}{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1} & {b}_{1} \\ {c}_{1} & 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{2} & {b}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{1}+{a}_{2} & {b}_{1}+{b}_{2} \\ {c}_{1}+{c}_{2} & 2\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned} $$ which is not a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is *not* closed under addition. - Statement II is false. If $A=\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & 1\end{bmatrix}$ is an element of $A,$ then $$ \begin{aligned}2A & =k\begin{bmatrix}a & b \\ c & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}2a & 2b \\ 2c & 2\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned} $$ which is not a matrix from $A.$ So, $A$ is *not* closed under scalar multiplication. - Statement III is false, while statement IV is true. $A$ is a *not* subspace because it's not closed under addition and scalar multiplication. Therefore, the correct answer is "IV only.""] ["question-63775110-b76b-5425-a979-1d472435c3ac" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a4c1e3e7-b7eb-5780-ac9f-e4101be00453" ["question-b7d1bf90-ec36-5fa3-9648-a21ed4abb91b" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,-1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1).$ So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,-1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}))\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}))\text{ }j \\ & =\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\text{ }i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(1,-1) & =\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\text{ }i+\frac{2(-1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\text{ }j \\ & =i-j\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we normalize $∇f(1,-1):$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,-1)}{‖∇f(1,-1)‖} & =\frac{i-j}{\sqrt{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\ & =\frac{i-j}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned} $$"] ["question-b7d1bf90-ec36-5fa3-9648-a21ed4abb91b" :question/difficulty ["question-ff3d7f48-7543-5dd7-9bd4-9af3c29d885b" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-2,0).$ So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0):$ $$ \begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\ & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}{e}^{xyz}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{xyz}+{y}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}{e}^{xyz}+{y}^{2})\,k \\ & =(2x+{x}^{2}yz){e}^{xyz}\,i+({x}^{3}z{e}^{xyz}+2y)\,j+{x}^{3}y{e}^{xyz}\,k \\ ∇f(1,-2,0) & =(2(1)+({1}^{2})(-2)(0)){e}^{1(-2)(0)}\,i+(({1}^{3})(0){e}^{1(-2)(0)}+2(-2))\,j+({1}^{3})(-2){e}^{1(-2)(0)}\,k \\ & =2\,i-4\,j-2\,k\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $2\,i-4\,j-2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$"] ["question-ff3d7f48-7543-5dd7-9bd4-9af3c29d885b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "question-ff3d7f48-7543-5dd7-9bd4-9af3c29d885b"] [17592186125740 :tutorial/content "The same property holds true in the case of three or more variables. In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if the gradient vector is nonzero, i.e., $$ \nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0, $$ then we have the following result: *$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$* To illustrate, let's consider the function $$ w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right). $$ The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$ The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get $$ \begin{aligned} \nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \\[5pt] &= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\\[5pt] &= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\\[10pt] \nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle. \end{aligned} $$ Now clearly, $\nabla f (0,0, 1)$ is perpendicular to $\mathcal S$ at the point $(0,0,1).$ ![](images/88/88bf25de31ae3318379865cdf2590c15216cb984cbf3948f975caa47317be664.png)"] ["question-e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45" :question/id #uuid "e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45"] ["question-e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45" :question/math-academy-id "q-225260"] ["question-e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45" :question/problem "**Fully** factor the following trinomial. $-12{a}^{2}-6a+6=$ {{field-1}}$(a\,+$ {{field-2}} $)($ {{field-3}} $a\,-1)$"] ["question-e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45" :question/worked-solution "We need to factor the following expression: $$ -12{a}^{2}-6a+6 $$ First, notice that all the terms have a common factor of $-6.$ So, we can simplify the calculation by first factoring out $-6:$ $$ \begin{aligned}-6(2{a}^{2}+a-1)\end{aligned} $$ Now, we just need to factor the trinomial $2{a}^{2}+a-1$ in parentheses. To do this, we find two numbers that - multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant (which is $2\times (-1)=-2$), and - add to the linear coefficient (which is $1$). The factor pairs of $-2$ are $$ (1,-2),\,(-1,2). $$ Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-1,2)$ add to $1:$ $$ -1+2=1\,✓ $$ Then, we write the linear term as $-a+2a,$ and factor the result by grouping: $$ \begin{aligned}2{a}^{2}+a-1 & = \\ 2{a}^{2}-a+2a-1 & = \\ (2{a}^{2}-a)+(2a-1) & = \\ a(2a-1)+(2a-1) & = \\ (a+1)(2a-1) & \end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the original trinomial factors as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}-12{a}^{2}-6a+6 & = \\ -6(2{a}^{2}+a-1) & = \\ -6(a+1)(2a-1) & \end{aligned} $$"] ["question-e8fb1410-51ee-5a0a-9a08-61072eaa2e45" :question/difficulty perimeter of the above triangle is $50+25\sqrt{2}.$ Find the measure of each leg."] ["question-7002a70c-d40e-53ed-9d27-c94492760a6a" :question/worked-solution "Because the triangle is isosceles, the legs must have the same length. Let $a$ be the length of each leg. So, we have $$ AB=BC=a. $$ Moreover, because the triangle is a *right* isosceles triangle, the hypotenuse must be equal to $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg. Therefore, $$ AC=AB\cdot \sqrt{2}=a\sqrt{2}. $$ Finally, since the perimeter is $p=50+25\sqrt{2},$ we have $$ \begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+AC \\ 50+25\sqrt{2} & =a+a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 25(2+\sqrt{2}) & =2a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 25(2+\sqrt{2}) & =(2+\sqrt{2})a \\ 25\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})} & =\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})}a \\ 25 & =a\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the measure of a leg is $25.$"] ["question-7f25e8cf-a84e-5491-8095-e34846bd72c0" :question/worked-solution "Our goal is to write the equation in the form $ax+by=c,$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors and $a\ge 0.$ We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side. This gives $$ -\frac{1}{5}x+y=2 $$ Now, we multiply both sides of the equation by $-1:$ $$ \begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}x+y & =2 \\ (-1)\cdot (-\frac{1}{5}x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (2) \\ \frac{1}{5}x-y & =-2.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, we multiply both sides of the equation by $5:$ $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}x-y & =-2 \\ 5\cdot (\frac{1}{5}x-y) & =5\cdot (-2) \\ x-5y & =-10.\end{aligned} $$ Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So we are done! The standard form of the line is $x-5y=-10.$"] ["question-7f25e8cf-a84e-5491-8095-e34846bd72c0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-dad8335d-f4a7-566b-a578-6ac7a63c8d7b" ["question-bf906107-b91f-584f-aecf-00f5767c9a3e" :question/worked-solution "The slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}).$ We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function $$ y=\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,u=2x. $$ Differentiating gives $$ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2. $$ We now apply the chain rule, and get $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\ & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡u)\cdot (2) \\ & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x).\end{aligned} $$ Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{8},$ we find $$ \begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{8}) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\ & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ & =2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ & =\sqrt{2}\,.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{8}$ is $\sqrt{2}.$"] ["question-bf906107-b91f-584f-aecf-00f5767c9a3e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-b1aeeb90-b252-58b0-bd1f-5b12f471387e" :question/problem "Find the truth set of the following predicate: $\,$ $P(x):$ ${x}^{2}-8=2x$ where the universal set is $R.$"] ["question-b1aeeb90-b252-58b0-bd1f-5b12f471387e" :question/worked-solution "The *truth set* of a predicate $P(x)$ is the set of elements in its universal set $U$ such that substituting these elements for the variable makes the predicate a true statement: $$ T=\{x\in U\,|\,P(x)\} $$ The universal set for our predicate is $U=R.$ We need to find $x\in U$ such that the following is true: $\,$ ${x}^{2}-8=2x$ Now, we solve the above equation by factoring: $$ \begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-8 & =2x \\ {x}^{2}-2x-8 & =0 \\ (x-4)(x+2) & =0\end{aligned} $$ So, the solutions are $x=-2\in R$ and $x=4\in R.$ Therefore, the truth set of our predicate is $T=\{-2,4\}.$"] ["question-b1aeeb90-b252-58b0-bd1f-5b12f471387e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-260f8856-8d02-57c2-89b0-9f4ad3929290" :question/worked-solution "The *truth set* $T$ of a predicate $P(x)$ is the set of elements in its universal set $U$ such that substituting these elements for the variable makes the predicate a true statement: $$ T=\{x\in U\,|\,P(x)\} $$ The universal set for our predicate is $$ U=\{5,6,…,20\}. $$ We need to find $x\in U$ such that the following is true: $\,$ $x$ is divisible by $3.$ The following numbers give the elements of our truth set: - $x=6$ since $6$ is divisible by $3,$ - $x=9$ since $9$ is divisible by $3,$ - $x=12$ since $12$ is divisible by $3,$ - $x=15$ since $15$ is divisible by $3,$ - $x=18$ since $18$ is divisible by $3.$ Therefore, the truth set of our predicate is $$ T=\{6,9,12,15,18\}. $$"] ["question-d193d524-b905-5ac6-8d71-b915f99a8936" :question/worked-solution "The *truth set* of a predicate $P({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})$ is the set of $n$-tuples in its universal set $U={U}_{1}\times {U}_{2}\times ⋯\times {U}_{n}$ such that substituting these tuples for the variables makes the predicate a true statement: $$ T=\{({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\in U\,|\,P({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\} $$ The universal set for our predicate is $$ \begin{aligned}U & =\{2,3\}\times \{5,8\} \\ & =\{(2,5),(2,8),(3,5),(3,8)\}.\end{aligned} $$ We need to find $(a,b)\in U$ such that the following is true: $\,$ $a+b$ is an odd number The following pairs give the elements of our truth set: - $(2,5)$ since $2+5=7$ and $7$ is an odd number, - $(3,8)$ since $3+8=11$ and $11$ is an odd number. \frac{y-1}{-2-1} & =\frac{x-(-1)}{2-(-1)} \\ \frac{y-1}{(-3)} & =\frac{x+1}{3} \\ y-1 & =-(x+1) \\ y & =-x.\end{aligned} $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =-{c}_{1}.\end{aligned} $$ Substituting the above into the equation ${c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=1,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1}-(-{c}_{1}) & =1 \\ 2{c}_{1} & =1 \\ {c}_{1} & segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $$ f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a). $$ Notice that the function $f(x,y)=y-{x}^{3}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem. Substituting $a=⟨-2,-8⟩$ and $b=⟨1,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get $$ \begin{aligned}f(1,0)-f(-2,-8) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,0⟩-⟨-2,-8⟩) \\ (0-{1}^{3})-(-8-(-2)^{3}) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,8⟩ \\ -1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨3,8⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-3{x}^{2},1⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-3{c}_{1}^{2},1⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $$ \begin{aligned}-1 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨3,8⟩ \\ -1 & =⟨-3{c}_{1}^{2},1⟩\cdot ⟨3,8⟩ \\ -1 & =-9{c}_{1}^{2}+8 \\ 9{c}_{1}^{2} & =9 \\ {c}_{1}^{2} & =1 \\ {c}_{1} & =\pm 1.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line. $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-(-8)}{0-(-8)} & =\frac{x-(-2)}{1-(-2)} \\ \frac{y+8}{8} & =\frac{x+2}{3} \\ y+8 & =\frac{8(x+2)}{3} \\ y & =\frac{8(x-1)}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{8({c}_{1}-1)}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem. - For ${c}_{1}=-1,$ we obtain $$ {c}_{2}=\frac{8(-1-1)}{3}=-\frac{16}{3}. $$ Therefore, the coordinates of the first point are $(-1,-\frac{16}{3}).$ - For ${c}_{1}=1,$ we obtain $$ {c}_{2}=\frac{8(1-1)}{3}=0. $$ Therefore, the coordinates of the second point are $(1,0).$ Finally we can conclude that the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem are $(-1,-\frac{16}{3})$ and $(1,0).$"] line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $$ f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a). $$ Notice that $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{3}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem. Substituting $a=⟨0,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,-1,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get $$ \begin{aligned}f(1,-1,0)-f(0,0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,-1,0⟩-⟨0,0,1⟩) \\ 1-(-1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 2 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨0,2y,-3{z}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨0,2{c}_{2},-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we get $$ \begin{aligned}2 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 2 & =⟨0,2{c}_{2},-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\ 2 & =-2{c}_{2}+3{c}_{3}^{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line. $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{(-1)}=\frac{z-1}{(-1)} \\ x & =-y=1-z\end{aligned} $$ Parametrizing the line, we get $$ x=t\,\,y=-t,\,z=1-t,\,0\le t\le 1. $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ {c}_{1}=t\,\,{c}_{2}=-t,\,{c}_{3}=1-t. $$ Substituting the above in the equation $-2{c}_{2}+3{c}_{3}^{2}=2,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}-2(-t)+3(1-t)^{2} & =2 \\ 2t+3{t}^{2}-6t+3 & =2 \\ 3{t}^{2}-4t+1 & =0 \\ (3t-1)(t-1) & =0 \\ t & =\frac{1}{3},\,1.\end{aligned} $$ Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem. - For $t=\frac{1}{3},$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}, \\ {c}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{3}, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, the coordinates of the first point $C$ are $(\frac{1}{3},-\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}).$ - For $t=1,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =1, \\ {c}_{2} & =-1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-1=0.\end{aligned} $$ Thus, the coordinates of the second point $C$ are $(1,-1,0).$"] ["question-aab55964-3387-5606-94f7-4fdb235f672a" :question/difficulty :question/problem "Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨-2,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨0,-2,0⟩,$ respectively."] ["question-6269cc62-3112-546a-8502-b50893c81d78" :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $$ f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a). $$ Notice that $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem. Substituting $a=⟨-2,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨0,-2,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get $$ \begin{aligned}f(0,-2,0)-f(-2,0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨0,-2,0⟩-⟨-2,0,1⟩) \\ -4-1 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩ \\ -5 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨0,-2y,2z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨0,-2{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, we get $$ \begin{aligned}-5 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩ \\ -5 & =⟨0,-2{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨2,-2,-1⟩ \\ -5 & =4{c}_{2}-2{c}_{3}.\end{aligned} $$ Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line. $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{x-(-2)}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{(-2)}=\frac{z-1}{(-1)} \\ \frac{x+2}{2} & =-\frac{y}{2}=1-z\end{aligned} $$ Parametrizing the line, we get $$ x=2t-2,\,y=-2t,\,z=1-t,\,0\le t\le 1. $$ Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have $$ {c}_{1}=2t-2,\,{c}_{2}=-2t,\,{c}_{3}=1-t. $$ Substituting the above in the equation $4{c}_{2}-2{c}_{3}=-5,$ we get $$ \begin{aligned}4(-2t)-2(1-t) & =-5 \\ -8t-2+2t & =-5 \\ -6t & =-3 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives $$ \begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =2(\frac{1}{2})-2=-1, \\ {c}_{2} & =-2(\frac{1}{2})=-1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned} $$ Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(-1,-1,\frac{1}{2}).$"] ["question-6269cc62-3112-546a-8502-b50893c81d78" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-8f422c3e-86d1-54ac-8460-f66bdadcbf77" :question/worked-solution "First, we notice that the function has precisely two distinct roots, $x=-1,$ and $x=3.$ Based on the graph, we can make the following conclusions about the multiplicities of the roots: - Since the graph just touches the $x$-axis and reverses direction at $x=-1,$ this root has even multiplicity. - Since the graph passes through $x=3,$ this root has odd multiplicity, and since the graph is tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=3,$ the multiplicity must be greater than one. From the given options, the only possible equation is $y=\frac{1}{9}(x+1)^{2}(x-3)^{3}.$"] ["question-8f422c3e-86d1-54ac-8460-f66bdadcbf77" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if the gradient vector is nonzero, i.e., $$ \nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0, $$ then we have the following result: *$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$* To illustrate, let's consider the function $$ w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right). $$ The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$ The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get $$ \eqalign{ \nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \[5pt] &= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\[5pt] &= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\[10pt] \nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle. } $$ Now clearly, $\nabla f (0,0, 1)$ is perpendicular to $\mathcal S$ at the point $(0,0,1).$ ![](images/88/88bf25de31ae3318379865cdf2590c15216cb984cbf3948f975caa47317be664.png)"] [17592186065335 :tutorial/content "The chain rule can be used to differentiate trigonometric functions like $$ y = \sin (2x). $$ First, notice that this function can be written as the composite function $$ y = \sin u, \qquad u = 2x. $$ We can use the chain rule to compute the derivative of this composite function: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\ & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(\operatorname{sin}u)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x) \\ & =\operatorname{cos}u\cdot 2 \\ & =2\operatorname{cos}u\end{aligned} $$ Substituting $u=2x,$ we obtain the final result: $$ \begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\operatorname{cos}(2x)\end{aligned} $$"] [17592186130324 :tutorial/content "Consider the graph of $$ y=\sqrt{x} $$ below. We will use this graph to compute $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 4} \sqrt{x} \,$. ![](images/e6/e6423b96ce60348e780ffd437207bdbeb456e3aae2888d7525f8c4e680f4ee43.png) From the graph, we see that as $x$ approaches $4$, the value of $y$ approaches $\sqrt{4}$. Therefore, $$ \lim\limits_{x\to 4} \sqrt{x} = \sqrt{4} = 2 $$ The limit of the square root function at a point is equal to the value of the square root function at that point, and this is true for any point *that is greater than $0$.* However, for points that are less than or equal to $0$, the limit does not exist: $$ lim_(x → c)\sqrt{x} = {\sqrt{c}\begin{vmatrix}ifc > 0 \\ DNE\end{vmatrix}ifc \le 0 $$ Why doesn't the limit exist for $$ c \leq 0 $$ ? - For $c < 0$, the limit $\lim\limits_{x \to \, c} \sqrt{x}$ does not exist because the square root function $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ is not defined for negative inputs. - Although $\sqrt{x}$ is defined at $x=0$, the left limit $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 0^-} \sqrt{x}$ does not exist because $\sqrt{x}$ is undefined left of $x=0$. Consequently, the overall limit $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 0} \sqrt{x}$ does not exist either."] [17592186130325 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to our plot of $$ y=\sqrt x $$ and work out its limits at infinity. ![](images/a0/a04b7cbc735c20a866b1d22287e2f3a1ffc247931c2de08c545cbd2fe922397b.png) As $x \to \infty$, the square root function increases without bound. So, we have $$ \lim_{x\to \infty}\sqrt{x} = \infty $$ On the other hand, when computing the limit as $x \to -\infty$, remember that the square root function isn't defined for $x<0$. Therefore, $$ \lim_{x\to -\infty}\sqrt{x} = \textrm{DNE} $$"] [17592186130326 :tutorial/content "Consider the graph of the cube root function $$ y=\sqrt[3]{x} $$ below. ![](images/20/20deb13b6bce6608c84db84472e19ade1d073c9562f4c414ebee36f4f9e9aebc.png) Unlike the square root function, the cube root is defined for all real $x$. As $x$ approaches any finite number $a$, the limit of the cube root function can be obtained by simply substituting $x=a$ into the cube root: $$ \lim_{x\to a} \sqrt[3]{x} = \sqrt[3]{a} $$ Additionally, we can see from the graph that the limits at infinity are $$ \lim_{x\to \infty} \sqrt[3]{x} = \infty \qquad \textrm{and}\qquad \lim_{x\to -\infty} \sqrt[3]{x} = -\infty $$"] [17592186065409 :tutorial/content "We know that the derivative of sine is cosine: $$ \dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(\sin{x}) = \cos{x} $$ Since integration is the reverse of differentiation, we see that the integral of cosine is sine: $$ \int \cos{x}\,\textrm d x = \sin{x} + C $$ We can discover two other integrals by considering the derivatives of cosine and tangent: $$ \begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cos}x+C \\ \int {sec}^{2}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{tan}x+C.\end{aligned} $$ Similarly, by considering the derivatives of secant, cosecant, and cotangent, we arrive at $$ \begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sec}x\operatorname{tan}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{sec}x+C \\ \int \operatorname{csc}x\operatorname{cot}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{csc}x+C \\ \int {csc}^{2}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cot}x+C.\end{aligned} $$ With these six formulas, we can integrate many different trigonometric functions."]]}

$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{3t}{e}^{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

$$

$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(3t) &={e}^{3t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{3t}.

$$

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t)={e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-2t)={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}(-2t){\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-2t{e}^{-2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}(1+2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2{e}^{-2t}t \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(2t) \\ -8{\alpha }_{1}t & =-8{e}^{-2t}t \\  & ={e}^{-2t}(-8t)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$"} {:db/id 17592186561040 :question/id #uuid "b34e24d7-8981-5c82-b39b-e245e3ef59b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-334730" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "939d48ec-1c25-5c44-bc01-35fa86ce8bd6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1-4t" :db/id 17592186560667}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186560667} :answer-field/id #uuid "5822d66e-2f18-53dd-b4cd-fb651a40362c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186560899} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bf58d67f-30ed-5d74-8536-0d89dad1de9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1+4t" :db/id 17592186560743}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186560743} :answer-field/id #uuid "7c222316-6984-59bf-8c22-0c5cad67de0d" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186560917}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Find ${e}^{At}$ for $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ -4 & 6\end{aligned}].$ 

*Hint: The only eigenvalue of $A$ is $2,$ and it has multiplicity two.*

<table align="l" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${e}^{At}={e}^{2t}\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">$4t$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center">$-4t$</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ -4 & 6\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 4{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -4{\alpha }_{1}t & 6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are functions to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-2{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1-4t), \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =6{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t}(1+4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{e}^{At}={e}^{2t}[\begin{aligned}1-4t & 4t \\ -4t & 1+4t\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186221411 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221194 :question/id #uuid "c0213c76-94e8-5ab3-a260-8a78a205589a" :question/math-academy-id "e-21724"} :knowledge-point/id
