equation of the normal line to the surface ${z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}z+y-\frac{\pi }{2}$ at the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y) & ={x}^{2}z+y-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ {z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)k \\  & =(2xy{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2xz)i+({x}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-1)j+(2z\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2})k \\ ∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =(2(-1)(\frac{\pi }{2})(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-2(-1)(1))i+((-1)^{2}(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-(-1)^{2})k \\  & =(-\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+2)i+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)k \\  & =2\,i-j+k \\  & =⟨2,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ and passes through the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)=⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,⟨2,-1,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186266052 :question/id #uuid "ec2f8828-cf4a-59b7-bf21-9952b961e912" :question/math-academy-id "q-131128"} {:db/id 17592186266053 :question/id #uuid "46c7ac33-5b38-5319-85fa-4f19aa20d07b" :question/math-academy-id "q-131130" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00dfea87-0564-54b8-b2ba-b85b9b81f898" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{4}=2-y=z-1" :db/id 17592186263009} {:answer/id #uuid "02bdc94f-aecb-598c-8c8e-fd84d09e16d7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=y-2=z-1" :db/id 17592186263024} {:answer/id #uuid "2143561b-a016-53c4-935f-4521d8cb87c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3=\frac{y-2}{2}=z-1" :db/id 17592186263298} {:answer/id #uuid "71e1bc5e-929a-5149-b69e-6390e2a09556" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-3}{2}=\frac{y-2}{4}=z-1" :db/id 17592186263985} {:answer/id #uuid "cd91307b-95b0-5c36-965f-60e3ce8f9695" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}" :db/id 17592186264798}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264798} :answer-field/id #uuid "3c8f2342-92e1-5c88-9098-f4db5aaee8bc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265357}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186338940 :question/id #uuid "5b6f2dff-79f7-5470-a733-d919ff7c2a24" :question/math-academy-id "q-71411"} {:db/id 17592186373006 :question/id #uuid "a1e0fe3a-1bd3-5ee4-ab1a-74e46b29c2c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-36351" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9dd151b9-79f9-5a66-8557-365b16a9535a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373008} {:answer/id #uuid "e407b4cd-b0e3-5ef2-a3e1-1c2c4a208e39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373009} {:answer/id #uuid "2042c239-c608-579c-a356-780f349dc015" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z" :db/id 17592186373010} {:answer/id #uuid "e11362e5-c68a-5d93-8627-d0fe7c1b9816" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y+1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373011} {:answer/id #uuid "dad753bd-efc6-5cc5-bf02-04d7fe01e2cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373012}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186373010} :answer-field/id #uuid "f074ec94-f4ab-59e4-98e4-6833b7d43d47" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186373007}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)$ at the point $(1,-1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z$, then our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,0).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)-z)k \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2x+y}\text{ }j-1\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{2(1)+(-1)}\text{ }j-k \\  & =2\text{ }i+\,j-k \\  & =⟨2,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by using the symmetric form of the equation of the line that is parallel to the vector $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$,  we get: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{1}=\frac{z-0}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186373139 :question/id #uuid "d41ffa1d-b743-559f-b433-9851a75bb790" :question/math-academy-id "q-71408" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124464 :knowledge-point/id #uuid :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,-1,1) & =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\  & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x \\ z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(\frac{1}{2},1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z-2{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}-x)k \\  & =(-4x-1)\text{ }i-4y\text{ }j+k \\ ∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3) & =(-4(\frac{1}{2})-1)\,i-4(1)\text{ }j+k \\  & =-3\,i-4\,j+k \\  & =⟨-3,-4,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ and passes through the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,∇f(\frac{1}{2},1,3)=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186405132 :question/id #uuid "a7c74ce4-3c4e-5ea4-ab88-89558065f279" :question/math-academy-id "q-36754" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id ${x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}=1$ at the point $(0,0,2),$ with parameter $t=0$ at this point." :question/worked-solution "First, note that we can write the equation of our surface as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,0,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{4}-1)k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+\frac{2y}{9}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{2}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,0,2) & =2(0)\text{ }i+\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }j+\frac{(2)}{2}\text{ }k \\  & =k \\  & =⟨0,0,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, the vector form of the equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(0,0,2)$ and passes through the point $(0,0,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨0,\,0,\,2⟩+t\,∇f(0,0,2)=⟨0,\,0,\,2⟩+t\,⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186497401 :question/id #uuid "ca2288f3-367d-50c0-9754-21f3665fdec7" :question/math-academy-id "q-71406" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id $$

$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186510365 :question/id #uuid "056dc885-9ad1-5245-b1aa-85becac66885" :question/math-academy-id "q-131125"} {:db/id 17592186510409 :question/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 1939} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125298 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

*$\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $C$ that passes through the point $P.$ *

This property is one of the most important facts in multivariable calculus since it gives a fundamental  link between
calculus and geometry!

Let's illustrate this property with a concrete example. Consider the paraboloid $z = f (x, y)=  x^2 + y^2$ and the level curve $\color{red}C$ of $f(x,y)$ corresponding to the point $P(1,-1).$  It is easy to see that  $\color{red}C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ with equation $x^2+y^2 = 2.$ 

![](images/f2/f2461dbfcde2403e6ed7de9d6288d33a4deb52319d35b7036628c3fa8b3789dc.png)

In this particular instance, the property says that

*$\nabla \! f(1,-1)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $\color{red}C$ that passes through the point $P(1,-1).$ *

![](images/48/481b68af522b9144e232d9c775f734cd998b31a21571cbfd983c23d0f68c3688.png)

Looking at the situation in the $xy$-plane, we see the following:

![](images/ce/ceb353d5164d6aa089a37e77c9469d747ef4430e363e42f9d35ee6d769d9a4e4.png)

Let's verify that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is a normal line to the level curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-1).$

- First, computing the gradient, we find that $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle.$ Therefore, 

$$
\nabla f(1,-1) = \langle 2, -2 \rangle.
$$

- Then, using elementary calculus, we can show that the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ is $y=x-2.$ Since this line has slope $m=1,$ it follows that the vector $\langle 1,1 \rangle$  is parallel to the level curve.

- Finally, taking the dot product between the gradient and the tangent vector, we obtain

$$
\nabla f(1,-1)\cdot  \langle 1,1 \rangle = \langle 2, -2\rangle \cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = 0.
$$

This means that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is *perpendicular* to the tangent line to $C$ at $(1,-1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68a96106-e224-5989-af04-8d464b6e58d5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2499 :tutorial/title 17592186125308 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125740 :tutorial/content "The same property holds true in the case of three or more variables. In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if  the  gradient vector is nonzero, i.e., 

$$
\nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0,
$$

then we have the following result:

*$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$*

17592186124731} {:db/id 17592186125298 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

*$\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $C$ that passes through the point $P.$ *

This property is one of the most important facts in multivariable calculus since it gives a fundamental  link between
calculus and geometry!

Let's illustrate this property with a concrete example. Consider the paraboloid $z = f (x, y)=  x^2 + y^2$ and the level curve $\color{red}C$ of $f(x,y)$ corresponding to the point $P(1,-1).$  It is easy to see that  $\color{red}C$ is a circle of radius $\sqrt{2}$ with equation $x^2+y^2 = 2.$ 

![](images/f2/f2461dbfcde2403e6ed7de9d6288d33a4deb52319d35b7036628c3fa8b3789dc.png)

In this particular instance, the property says that

*$\nabla \! f(1,-1)$ is a normal vector to the level curve $\color{red}C$ that passes through the point $P(1,-1).$ *

![](images/48/481b68af522b9144e232d9c775f734cd998b31a21571cbfd983c23d0f68c3688.png)

Looking at the situation in the $xy$-plane, we see the following:

![](images/ce/ceb353d5164d6aa089a37e77c9469d747ef4430e363e42f9d35ee6d769d9a4e4.png)

Let's verify that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is a normal line to the level curve $C$ at the point $P(1,-1).$

- First, computing the gradient, we find that $\nabla f = \langle 2x, 2y \rangle.$ Therefore, 

$$
\nabla f(1,-1) = \langle 2, -2 \rangle.
$$

- Then, using elementary calculus, we can show that the equation of the tangent to $C$ at $P$ is $y=x-2.$ Since this line has slope $m=1,$ it follows that the vector $\langle 1,1 \rangle$  is parallel to the level curve.

- Finally, taking the dot product between the gradient and the tangent vector, we obtain

$$
\nabla f(1,-1)\cdot  \langle 1,1 \rangle = \langle 2, -2\rangle \cdot \langle 1,1 \rangle = 0.
$$

This means that $\nabla f(1,-1)$ is *perpendicular* to the tangent line to $C$ at $(1,-1).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "68a96106-e224-5989-af04-8d464b6e58d5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2499 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "35b375f8-a01b-56db-97b7-ac88f2a7883a" :step/math-academy-id 11200 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125306}} {:db/id 17592186125735 :tutorial/content "Given a function $z=f(x,y)$, if both partial derivatives $f_x,$ $f_y$ exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a point $P(x_0,y_0)$ in the domain of the function, and if $\nabla \! f(x_0,y_0) \neq \mathbf 0,$ then we have the following result:

In general, if $f$ is a differentiable real-valued function of $n$ variables, $\mathbf y$ is a point in the domain of $f,$ and if  the  gradient vector is nonzero, i.e., 

$$
\nabla f (\mathbf y)= \left \langle f_{x_1}(\mathbf y), f_{x_2}(\mathbf y), \cdots, f_{x_n}(\mathbf y)\right \rangle \neq \mathbf 0,
$$

then we have the following result:

*$\nabla f (\mathbf y)$ is a normal vector to the level surface $f(x_1,x_2, \cdots, x_n) =f(\mathbf y)$ at $\mathbf y.$*

To illustrate, let's consider the function  

$$
w = f (x, y, z)= \dfrac 1 2\left(x^2 + y^2 + z^2-1\right).
$$

 

The level surface corresponding to $w=0$ is the sphere $\mathcal S$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 +z^2 =1.$ 

The point $P(0,0,1)$ lies on $\mathcal S.$ Computing $\nabla f(0,0,1),$ we get

$$
\eqalign{
\nabla f(x,y,z) &= \langle f_x, \: f_y, \:f_z\rangle \[5pt]
&= \dfrac12\langle2x, \: 2y, \: 2z\rangle\[5pt]
&= \langle x, \: y, \: z\rangle\[10pt]

\nabla f(0,0,1) &= \langle 0,\: 0,\: 1 \rangle.
}
$$

Now clearly, $\nabla f (0,0, 1)$ is perpendicular to $\mathcal S$ at the point $(0,0,1).$

perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-2,-3,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}-xy)\,k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-2,-3,1) & =(4(-2)-(-3))\,i-(-2)\,j+2(1)\,k \\  & =-5\,i+2\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-5\,i+2\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-2,-3,1).$"} :step/id #uuid "6c546df4-95bc-53a6-8314-f63e977926a5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406789}} {:db/id 17592186406789 :step/content {:db/id 17592186406787 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a1d5e01-e81c-5544-a929-055747dc7f77" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-3=0" :db/id 17592186406774} {:answer/id #uuid "82778c6a-7758-50ec-ad08-3720a9d490ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-3=0" :db/id 17592186406777} {:answer/id #uuid "cdae5c41-27fa-5c55-9f46-cceeabd59a1a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y-5=0" :db/id 17592186406779} {:answer/id #uuid "dbcc8cce-7237-5eb6-ac41-6a5901ea8c81" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-4=0" :db/id 17592186406780} {:answer/id #uuid "ecf6508f-66f3-52c3-8fbf-477ac88383db" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y-1=0" :db/id 17592186406783}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186406779} :answer-field/id #uuid "f9e7ba4e-7d61-5628-8ce5-894dfba410f8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186406785}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ef115c0b-3981-5c8f-8e9d-f41c20799c2d" :question/math-academy-id "q-130719" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $2y-x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}).$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{x}{2y})-2y+x,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,1):$

\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,-1,1) & =2(-1)\text{ }i+2(-1)\text{ }j+2(1)\text{ }k \\  & =-2\,i-2\,j+2\,k \\  & =⟨-2,-2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{-2}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y+1}{1}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ x+1=y+1=\frac{z-1}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "20ee70ca-88be-504d-b7aa-237d8d22e58a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186423054}} {:db/id 17592186423054 :step/content {:db/id 17592186423051 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "364ddf2b-cdd1-5e21-88c2-478a7d637e32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+3y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423045} {:answer/id #uuid "415a3975-289f-5c0a-aa48-bc85b813f82a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y-4=0" :db/id 17592186423046} {:answer/id #uuid "6321cb0e-8e68-5a7b-9a36-ac871cc17b89" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423047} {:answer/id #uuid "82ce7cc2-be21-5dc4-9b04-e941ddd03d24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423048} {:answer/id #uuid "ba63a292-9d83-540d-ac68-00ce4812ebb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-2=0" :db/id 17592186423049}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186423048} :answer-field/id #uuid "02401848-522e-501b-82ff-6e5cb3f48ab9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186423050}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6f16c0b1-b80b-5067-adaf-a65b04fb7bb4" :question/math-academy-id "q-130721" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${e}^{{x}^{2}y}={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{2}y} & ={y}^{2}-{x}^{3}+9 \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3} & =9\end{aligned}

If we set $f(x,y)={e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=9.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{{x}^{2}y}-{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})j \\  & =(2xy{e}^{{x}^{2}y}+3{x}^{2})i+({x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{2}y}-2y)j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =(2(2)(0){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}+3({2}^{2}))i+(({2}^{2}){e}^{({2}^{2})(0)}-2(0))j \\  & =12\,i+4\,j \\  & =⟨12,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨12,4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{12} & =\frac{y-0}{4} \\ 4(x-2) & =12y \\ x-2 & =3y \\ x-3y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "68e1c4ea-40a6-5a21-ae75-071da89109f6" :step/next {:db/id 17592186423052}} {:db/id 17592186423055 :step/content {:db/id 17592186373006 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "9dd151b9-79f9-5a66-8557-365b16a9535a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y+1}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373008} {:answer/id #uuid "e407b4cd-b0e3-5ef2-a3e1-1c2c4a208e39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y}{2}=-z" :db/id 17592186373009} {:answer/id #uuid "2042c239-c608-579c-a356-780f349dc015" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x-1}{2}=y+1=-z" :db/id 17592186373010} {:answer/id #uuid "e11362e5-c68a-5d93-8627-d0fe7c1b9816" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-1=\frac{y+1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373011} {:answer/id #uuid "dad753bd-efc6-5cc5-bf02-04d7fe01e2cb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{x+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{2}=z" :db/id 17592186373012}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186373010} :answer-field/id #uuid "f074ec94-f4ab-59e4-98e4-6833b7d43d47" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186373007}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "a1e0fe3a-1bd3-5ee4-ab1a-74e46b29c2c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-36351" :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y)$ at the point $(1,-1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} :step/id #uuid "bf1f0a54-a2e4-5d5b-9366-b7874e2b2325" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497425}}] :activity/title "The Gradient as a Normal Vector" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident :activity.type/review} :db/id 17592186496648} {:db/id 17592186497419 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125190 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "034d9a67-8763-5c70-b5b9-7febdebfdaf9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x-5y+1=0" :db/id 17592186496664} {:answer/id #uuid "132dcf6f-8423-544a-b9b0-4fe0220a1869" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-x-3y+5=0" :db/id 17592186496700} {:answer/id #uuid "6cc0248f-f177-570e-9398-26b743d6c5ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2x-2y+3=0" :db/id 17592186496894} {:answer/id #uuid "9a929f5c-99d1-523a-aabc-fdf5eb4c7f18" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x+5y-3=0" :db/id 17592186496982} {:answer/id #uuid "bc272b8f-4ab5-5f01-8506-f12b4f57de0b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5x-4y+1=0" :db/id 17592186497043}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186496982} :answer-field/id #uuid "22b9919e-c058-55c4-a73e-14ca053dbdce" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186123740}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "cb219d72-040d-55dd-90ca-3f831acb4d64" :question/math-academy-id "q-65173" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve $xy={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-7.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,-1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$

$$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$

:question/math-academy-id "q-71406" :question/problem "Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz$ at the point $(1,0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)-xyz \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2)\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2).$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y+z)+xyz)k \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+yz)\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xz)\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{x+y+z}+xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,1) & =(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(0)(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(1))\text{ }j+(\frac{1}{1+0+1}+(1)(0))\,k \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{3}{2}\,j+\frac{1}{2}\,k \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,0,1)$ and passes through the point $(1,0,1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,∇f(1,0,1)=⟨1,0,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$"} :step/id #uuid "bf1f0a54-a2e4-5d5b-9366-b7874e2b2325" :step/next {:db/id 17592186497425}} {:db/id 17592186497425 :step/content {:db/id 17592186265960 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "076ccae2-d102-5ad8-b1c2-ac28978e3e97" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-3y=0" :db/id 17592186263068} {:answer/id #uuid "1b3882de-2108-52bf-b5e1-4c3304b9a5c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-y-2=0" :db/id 17592186263257} {:answer/id #uuid "a00ce4f7-3888-5dba-a972-b715615f1421" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-4=0" :db/id 17592186264362} {:answer/id #uuid "cf2a0770-0459-500c-aa32-352ae1667e03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+3y-6=0" :db/id 17592186264813} {:answer/id #uuid "d493ac59-d9ae-5896-bd9e-006d111d56b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y-7=0" :db/id 17592186264850}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264362} :answer-field/id #uuid "cb7e101e-fe81-5db4-a578-c892744685d7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265605}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c80428ab-daca-506e-aca7-d4e40b0d604c" :question/math-academy-id "q-130718" :question/problem "Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}=6.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(3,1).$" :question/worked-solution "If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-3{y}^{2},$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=6.$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i-6y\,j \\ ∇f(3,1) & =2(3)\,i-6(1)\,j \\  & =6\,i-6\,j \\  & =⟨6,-6⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(3,1)=⟨6,-6⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(3,1).$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,-1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,-1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-xy-7)\,j \\  & =(2x-y)\,i+(2y-x)\,j \\ ∇f(2,-1) & =(2(2)-(-1))\,i+(2(-1)-2)\,j \\  & =5\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,-1)=⟨5,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,-1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-2}{5} & =\frac{y-(-1)}{-4} \\ -4(x-2) & =5(y+1) \\ -4x-5y+8-5 & =0 \\ -4x-5y+3 & =0 \\ 4x+5y-3 & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}{y}^{2} & =2x+y \\ {x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}-2x-y)j \\  & =(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-2)\,i+(2{x}^{3}y-1)\,j \\ ∇f(-1,1) & =(3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}-2)\,i+(2(-1)^{3}(1)-1)\,j \\  & =\,i-3\,j \\  & =⟨1,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(-1,1)=⟨1,-3⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-1}{(-3)} \\ -3(x+1) & =y-1 \\ -3x-3 & =y-1 \\ 3x+y+2 & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(0,-1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,-1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)+{y}^{2}-z)k \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\text{ }i+(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)+2y)\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(0,-1,1) & =(-1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)\text{ }i+[(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+2(-1)]\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =-i-2\,j-k \\  & =⟨-1,-2,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1}=\frac{y-(-1)}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{-1}=\frac{y+1}{-2}=\frac{z-1}{-1} \\ \frac{x}{1}=\frac{y+1}{2}=\frac{z-1}{1} \\ x=\frac{y+1}{2}=z-1\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "2598a4b3-3e2b-55cf-8762-35fa24bff20e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186527256}} {:db/id 17592186527235 :step/content {:db/id 17592186403468 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "74e84be6-fb21-5888-bde0-2b1fc8861800" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨-3,-4,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩" :db/id 17592186403470} {:answer/id #uuid "125b86ba-8a17-5cc7-bb9b-688c88040c9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨3,-4,1⟩+t\,⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩" :db/id 17592186403471} {:answer/id #uuid "a563a551-487d-52b0-b121-65d93d53f35f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨3,4,1⟩" :db/id 17592186403472} {:answer/id #uuid "74e61dbd-b0b0-51fb-aee1-a797c08c8fb2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨3,-4,1⟩" :db/id 17592186403473} {:answer/id #uuid "65d0bd41-c0f7-5813-a9d5-53b92a3b0d8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "r=⟨\frac{1}{2},1,3⟩+t\,⟨-3,-4,1⟩" :db/id 17592186403474}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186403474} :answer-field/id #uuid "3a86f3ea-971f-5c0c-ab0d-7a86359ca0e2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186403469}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ca7dad4d-8007-5c21-9019-38d66b5366c7" :question/math-academy-id "q-71407" :question/problem "Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface $z=2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},1,3).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$

${lim}_{t\to -1}(\sqrt[7]{(2t+1)^{7}}-\sqrt[3]{({t}^{2}+t+1)^{6}})=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Applying the sum and root rules, we get

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to -1}(\sqrt[7]{(2t+1)^{7}}-\sqrt[3]{({t}^{2}+t+1)^{6}}) & ={lim}_{t\to -1}\sqrt[7]{(2t+1)^{7}}-{lim}_{t\to -1}\sqrt[3]{({t}^{2}+t+1)^{6}} \\  & =\sqrt[7]{{({lim}_{t\to -1}(2t+1))}^{7}}-\sqrt[3]{{({lim}_{t\to -1}({t}^{2}+t+1))}^{6}} \\  & =\sqrt[7]{(2(-1)+1)^{7}}-\sqrt[3]{(((-1)^{2}+(-1)+1))^{6}} \\  & =\sqrt[7]{(-2+1)^{7}}-\sqrt[3]{((1-1+1))^{6}} \\  & =\sqrt[7]{(-1)^{7}}-\sqrt[3]{(1)^{6}} \\  & =\sqrt[7]{-1}-\sqrt[3]{1} \\  & =-1-1 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186563742 :question/id #uuid "d591e3b7-0993-5fb9-b7f0-ff97c33bf559" :question/math-academy-id "q-100250" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "16ba1e29-25ac-579d-9cfe-24448c56edab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186562995} {:answer/id #uuid "a0bf2b88-34c6-53e4-a455-89e06f7f9a7a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186563306} {:answer/id #uuid "db467dc8-4b26-512d-821f-e3c4973e9fd6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt[3]{6}" :db/id 17592186563426} {:answer/id #uuid "fbdaaac8-b49f-51b4-b323-7ea59a4fdd9d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{2}}" :db/id 17592186563510} {:answer/id #uuid "ff7f4802-e1a5-55e2-9352-05637b9f8392" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186563516}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186563516} :answer-field/id #uuid "ddff0f96-aeb7-5490-8d56-4c8b9d0de231" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186563630}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find ${lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}.$" :question/worked-solution "Applying the quotient rule, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to 2}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}=\frac{{lim}_{x\to 2}3x}{{lim}_{x\to 2}\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}}
$$

We calculate the limits of the numerator and denominator, separately.

For the numerator, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}3x & =3{lim}_{x\to 2}x \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the root rule in the denominator, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 2}\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5} & =\sqrt[3]{{lim}_{x\to 2}(2{x}^{4}-5)} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{2(2)^{4}-5)} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{27} \\  & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{3x}{\sqrt[3]{2{x}^{4}-5}} & =\frac{6}{3}=2\,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186054605 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186054519 :question/id #uuid "3d6b32ee-3385-5fba-91a5-66c0bbb13dea" :question/math-academy-id "e-3565"} :knowledge-point/id "![](images/b7/b75586450ddee4f682f02539e02462d0aa5f88830b2989cc7cc2f4f6df635ade.png)

Find ${lim}_{x\to \,-1}(5+7x)^{3}(f(x)-x)^{4}$ for the function $f(x)$ plotted above." :question/worked-solution "From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to \,-1}f(x)=0.$ 

From the product rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-1}(5+7x)^{3}(f(x)-x)^{4}={lim}_{x\to \,-1}(5+7x)^{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,-1}(f(x)-x)^{4}.
$$

We calculate the limits of each factor, separately.

Applying the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-1}(5+7x)^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,-1}(5+7x))}^{3} \\  & =(5+7\cdot (-1))^{3} \\  & =(-2)^{3} \\  & =-8,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-1}(f(x)-x)^{4} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,-1}(f(x)-x))}^{4} \\  & =(0-(-1))^{4} \\  & ={1}^{4} \\  & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,-1}(5+7x)^{3}(f(x)-x)^{4} & ={lim}_{x\to \,-1}(5+7x)^{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,-1}(f(x)-x)^{4} \\  & =(-8)\cdot (1) \\  & =-8\,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186055234 :question/id #uuid "2ac5072a-3fbc-59dc-8124-c0a14abf22a5" :question/math-academy-id "q-35616"} {:db/id 17592186233023 :question/id #uuid "98c65517-e27d-5eb7-b458-8dcf5425928f" :question/math-academy-id "q-100273" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b2d9170-72bf-5608-bc85-b7e1e90b7337" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186533246} {:answer/id #uuid "3a9642e4-5571-5f69-b42d-8a766a19f94a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186533276} {:answer/id #uuid "b3087c4f-f3ff-5f73-85e3-80711023e115" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" :db/id 17592186533572} {:answer/id #uuid "c97fc178-695e-5644-8659-728e66bdb6d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186533621} {:answer/id #uuid "cfdaab07-184b-57e0-83cf-49eb37899d71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186533643}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533276} :answer-field/id #uuid "eccb0955-0665-53a1-96c5-95a613de628c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186533947}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/fd/fda731fa3c9a3401e9b9e2a7d4c103829d3fe3b14ac9d6f2872b76a319f6ae91.png)

Find ${lim}_{x\to \,1}(2{x}^{3}-4f(x))^{3}(2{x}^{4}-3)^{2}$ for the function $f(x)$ plotted above." :question/worked-solution "From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to \,1}f(x)=1.$ 

From the product rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,1}(2{x}^{3}-4f(x))^{3}(2{x}^{4}-3)^{2}={lim}_{x\to \,1}(2{x}^{3}-4f(x))^{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,1}(2{x}^{4}-3)^{2}.
$$

We calculate the limits of each factor, separately.

Applying the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}(2{x}^{3}-4f(x))^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,1}(2{x}^{3}-4f(x)))}^{3} \\  & =(2(1)^{3}-4(1))^{3} \\  & =(-2)^{3} \\  & =-8,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}(2{x}^{4}-3)^{2} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,1}(2{x}^{4}-3))}^{2} \\  & =(2(1)^{4}-3)^{2} \\  & =(-1)^{2} \\  & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,1}(2{x}^{3}-4f(x))^{3}(2{x}^{4}-3)^{2} & ={lim}_{x\to \,1}(2{x}^{3}-4f(x))^{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,1}(2{x}^{4}-3)^{2} \\  & =(-8)\cdot (1) \\  & =-8\,.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186233024 :question/id #uuid "cf0e9385-58bd-5390-aec9-13a595f379a8" :question/math-academy-id "q-100275"} {:db/id 17592186233025 :question/id #uuid If the figure above shows the graph of the function $f(x),$ then

${lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\,(f(x)-2)^{3}=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to \,2}f(x)=3.$

From the product rule, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\,(f(x)-2)^{3}={lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2)^{3}.
$$

We calculate the limits of each factor, separately.

Applying the power rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1))}^{2} \\  & =(2-1)^{2} \\  & ={1}^{2} \\  & =1\,,\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2)^{3} & ={({lim}_{x\to \,2}(f(x)-2))}^{3} \\  & =(3-2)^{3} \\  & ={1}^{3} \\  & =1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,2}(x-1)^{2}\,(f(x)-2)^{3} & =(1)\cdot (1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048435 :topic/id #uuid "9f05a2f3-96ce-5d8f-a6a0-1494c05fed7e" :topic/knowledge-points [{:db/id 17592186129195 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186129023 each leg?" :question/worked-solution "The hypotenuse in a ${45}^{∘}$-${45}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle is equal to $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg.

Here, we know that the hypotenuse has length $2.$ So, if the length of a leg is $a,$ then we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\sqrt{2}\cdot a \\ a & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the square root from the denominator, we can multiply both the numerator and denominator by $\sqrt{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =\frac{2\cdot \sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the length of each leg is $\sqrt{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186059636 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059464 :question/id #uuid "0d244991-c12e-5c56-8f58-762d8be22f8a" The perimeter of the above triangle is $10+5\sqrt{2}.$ Find the measure of each leg." :question/worked-solution "Because the triangle is isosceles, the legs must have the same length. Let $a$ be the length of each leg. So, we have

$$
AB=BC=a.
$$

Moreover, because the triangle is a *right* isosceles triangle, the hypotenuse must be equal to $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg. Therefore,

$$
AC=AB\cdot \sqrt{2}=a\sqrt{2}.
$$

Finally, since the perimeter is $p=10+5\sqrt{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+AC \\ 10+5\sqrt{2} & =a+a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 5(2+\sqrt{2}) & =2a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 5(2+\sqrt{2}) & =(2+\sqrt{2})a \\ 5\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})} & =\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})}a \\ 5 & =a.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the measure of a leg is $5.$"} {:db/id 17592186508113 :question/id #uuid "ed931f9b-ec89-504b-8f3a-6fc6233992c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-82302" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "32fcd00f-a39a-58b1-925b-6f97038dc7ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186507668} {:answer/id #uuid "7a5e9904-c441-5249-95eb-da32c2bf31f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186507775} {:answer/id #uuid "b21ebaaf-7316-5810-a179-40920135f9f4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186507844} {:answer/id #uuid "e5291e91-5e75-563e-9047-4ac169fda707" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186507908} {:answer/id #uuid "fa1bd1ce-5d7c-5356-8a41-6149fd10be2a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186507937}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186507937} :answer-field/id #uuid "563ab28a-360a-5519-9504-d8c10d6a3bc9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186507979}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/27/2788f2795065599063c67d9ae7e9e6ee17cae4aa21198450faf7c09ad10765e1.png)

$(3{s}^{2}+2s+4)({s}^{2}+3s+2)=3{s}^{4}+a{s}^{3}+b{s}^{2}+cs+8,$ calculate $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "We distribute all three terms of the trinomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3{s}^{2}+2s+4)({s}^{2}+3s+2) & = \\ 3{s}^{2}({s}^{2}+3s+2)+(2s)({s}^{2}+3s+2)+(4)({s}^{2}+3s+2) & = \\ 3{s}^{4}+9{s}^{3}+6{s}^{2}+2{s}^{3}+6{s}^{2}+4s+4{s}^{2}+12s+8 & = \\ 3{s}^{4}+11{s}^{3}+16{s}^{2}+16s+8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=11,$ $b=16,$ and $c=16.$ So,

{:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186085125}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Express the equation of the line $y=-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{1}{2}$ in standard form.

{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "Our goal is to write the equation in the form $ax+by=c,$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors and $a\ge 0.$

We begin by moving all of the variables to the left-hand side and all of the constants to the right-hand side. This gives

$$
\frac{1}{5}x+y=\frac{1}{2}
$$

Now, we multiply both sides of the equation by $10:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}x+y & =\frac{1}{2} \\ 10\cdot (\frac{1}{5}x+y) & =10\cdot (\frac{1}{2}) \\ 2x+10y & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors, and $a\ge 0.$ So we are done!

The standard form of the line is 

$$
2x+10y=5.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186088299 :question/id #uuid "135eff31-3e85-5950-8586-d76c428cdfbc" :question/math-academy-id "q-7374"} {:db/id 17592186088300 :question/id #uuid "1ddc1b00-1388-5ab1-b4ec-fe79f4a369ed" :question/math-academy-id "q-7375" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3ce635f8-4383-5e2d-baa8-462f0646a57d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=2x-10" :db/id 17592186525359} {:answer/id #uuid "56dcaada-2e45-5e47-b10d-7423de786283" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y-2x=10" :db/id 17592186525431} {:answer/id #uuid "a64fc9d9-1954-54bb-9104-2c70061145e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y=10" :db/id 17592186525626} {:answer/id #uuid "a9fc8576-442e-5448-9c72-26dd2ff8c409" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y=10" :db/id 17592186525635} {:answer/id #uuid "b0e5661e-64af-5f76-ad7e-bb04261a05bc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y-10=0" :db/id 17592186525654}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186525635} :answer-field/id #uuid "8bedc031-1af4-59be-8827-ddccc40055ed" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186086454}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Write $y=2x-10$ in standard form." :question/worked-solution "Our goal is to write the equation in the form $ax+by=c,$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers with no common factors and $a\ge 0.$

form?" :question/worked-solution "First, we will construct the point-slope form of the line. Then, we will simplify it into standard form.

To construct the point-slope form of the line, we need a point and a slope. We already have two points, so we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{7-0}{4-0}=\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use this slope along with one of the points to write the point-slope form equation of the line. It doesn't matter which point we choose, but let's choose $(0,0).$ The point-slope equation is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =\frac{7}{4}(x-0) \\ y & =\frac{7}{4}x\end{aligned}
$$

To simplify the point-slope formula into standard form, we first multiply by $4$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{7}{4}(x) \\ 4\cdot (y) & =4\cdot \frac{7}{4}(x) \\ 4y & =7x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we move the variables to the left side and the constant to the right side:

$$
\begin{aligned}4y & =7x \\ -7x+4y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply by $-1$ to make the $x$-coefficient positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}-7x+4y & =0 \\ (-1)\cdot (-7x+4y) & =(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 7x-4y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the standard form of the equation is $7x-4y=0.$"} {:db/id 17592186501213 :question/id #uuid "b34b9e0f-ca1a-53ee-8948-5e07722771b6" :question/math-academy-id "q-72425" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aa1d2cc4-2934-5c01-acf3-e4688de64dff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x-y=6" :db/id 17592186500819} {:answer/id #uuid "c0d0840e-b8f1-5833-899d-775ab6668a32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-y=3" :db/id 17592186500867} {:answer/id #uuid "c3d3f7b4-e921-553d-88ad-be60876e12b6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=2x-3" :db/id 17592186500877} {:answer/id #uuid "ca9d0db1-1d42-546b-8c61-bc0bc89d225c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4x+y=-6" :db/id 17592186500896} {:answer/id #uuid "cf99202c-1f33-5c86-9aa3-ff042e4be5ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y=4" :db/id 17592186500913}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186500819} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ee1d5f3-79b0-529f-9d27-584c54dd513d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186501034}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "What is the equation of the line that passes through the points $(1,-2)$ and $(3,6)$, expressed in standard form?" :question/worked-solution "First, we will construct the point-slope form of the line. To construct the point-slope form of the line, we need a point and a slope. We already have two points, so we calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{6-(-2)}{3-1}=\frac{8}{2}=4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use this slope along with one of the points to write the point-slope form equation of the line. It doesn't matter which point we choose, but let's choose $(1,-2).$ The point-slope equation is as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-2) & =4(x-1) \\ y+2 & =4(x-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we simplify the point-slope formula into standard form, moving the variables to the left side and the constant to the right side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2 & =4(x-1) \\ y+2 & =4x-4 \\ y & =4x-6 \\ -4x+y & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply by $-1$ to make the $x$-coefficient positive:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4x+y & =-6 \\ (-1)\cdot (-4x+y) & =(-1)\cdot (-6) \\ 4x-y & =6\end{aligned}
$$

So, the standard form of the equation is $4x-y=6.$"} {:db/id 17592186048936} {:db/id 17592186049169} {:db/id 17592186049201} {:db/id 17592186049869} {:db/id 17592186050320} {:db/id 17592186049388 (Figure not drawn to scale)" :question/worked-solution "The area of the triangle is defined as 

$$
A=\frac{b\cdot h}{2},
$$

 where $b$ is the base and $h$ is the corresponding height.

From the diagram, we see that the height is $h=BM,$ and the corresponding base is 

$$
b=AM+MC=14\,cm.
$$

Therefore, using the formula for the area, we can solve for the height as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{b\cdot h}{2} \\ 49 & =\frac{14\cdot h}{2} \\ 98 & =14\cdot h \\ h & =\frac{98}{14} \\ h & =7\,cm\end{aligned}
$$

What is the baby's unit rate of growth?" :question/worked-solution "The baby's unit rate of growth in centimeters per month is simply the constant of proportionality for the given proportional relationship.

To compute the constant of proportionality, we first need to choose a point $(x,y)$ on the graph. Here, let's choose the point $(2,5).$

![](images/5b/5bbc6c5b4188c5db894ceebe7d347c901afb428d5d102864a90218ef53420a60.png)

Now, we can find the constant of proportionality by computing the ratio of the $y$-coordinate to the $x$-coordinate, as follows:

$$
k=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{5}{2}
$$

$$

$$

$$
\frac{4}{3}=1\,\text{R}1=1\,\frac{1}{3}
$$

The graph above shows a direct variation between the variables $y$ and $x.$ Which equation describes the relationship between the variables?" :question/worked-solution "Since $y$ varies directly with $x,$ we use the equation

$$
y=kx.
$$

Next, we notice there is a point on the graph with $y=8$ and $x=2.$ So, we substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =k\cdot 2 \\ \frac{8}{2} & =k \\ 4 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
y=4x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186152868 :question/id #uuid "606876d0-48a2-5ca9-a29f-57916ecc5e18" :question/math-academy-id "q-91837"} {:db/id 17592186498511 :question/id #uuid "2f89b123-1c77-5362-ac5f-d71cbdc1fae2" :question/math-academy-id "q-115616"} {:db/id 17592186498547 :question/id #uuid "700640db-e0fe-571f-9cca-6b3afdd864a7" :question/math-academy-id "q-51877"} {:db/id 17592186520477 :question/id #uuid "817c5709-21ea-5c46-9e06-c595f5917c73" :question/math-academy-id "q-68204" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2dd7620a-2e0a-5048-84e8-580582cc4050" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\frac{3}{2}x" :db/id 17592186520060} {:answer/id #uuid "5c1e780f-72c4-55fe-86bf-f63cbb6742d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\frac{1}{4}x" :db/id 17592186520134} {:answer/id #uuid "67143172-5c75-57e2-9507-5548168537b5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\frac{2}{3}x" :db/id 17592186520148} {:answer/id #uuid "8052a59d-160b-523d-93b3-2be518aa22c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=\frac{1}{3}x" :db/id 17592186520175} {:answer/id #uuid "faaf0326-bcd6-5fdb-9b82-fb8c891b09c7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y=3x" :db/id 17592186520359}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186520175} :answer-field/id #uuid "df70821b-247b-5776-8c45-aa8d80611751" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186520434}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/1a/1a5313995e9740a61b455a9c368aca6223a80c8bbea659f06ec2a63c8260747b.png)

Karen decides to walk from her workplace to her house. There is a proportional relationship between the distance $x$ (in kilometers) she covers and the time $y$ (in hours) it takes her to cover that distance.

What is the equation for the relationship between $x$ and $y$ shown in the graph above?" :question/worked-solution "Every proportional relationship takes the form $y=kx,$ where $k$ is the constant of proportionality.

To compute the constant of proportionality, we first need to choose a point $(x,y)$ on the graph. Here, let's choose the point $(3,1).$

![](images/be/bec01f9dc01b340075f09dd459571fe8199116f18a6ab912eb958c7a6f9ee4f2.png)

Now, we can find the constant of proportionality by computing the ratio of the $y$-coordinate to the $x$-coordinate, as follows:

$$
k=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

Therefore, the equation is

$$
y=\frac{1}{3}x.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186572691 :question/id #uuid "528c6dbc-6dbe-5499-88b0-b6881a756455" :question/math-academy-id "q-115639" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a10968a-1243-571b-a9bd-8c6631c847bb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "u=-\frac{1}{2}z" :db/id 17592186572345} {:answer/id #uuid "440df762-731d-56df-bc2f-7e0b6dfe87dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "u=\frac{1}{5}z" :db/id 17592186572398} {:answer/id #uuid "81b9413e-71d2-55bc-b120-48cf7418e25a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "u=-5z" :db/id 17592186572455} {:answer/id #uuid "bbcec67a-21f7-515b-b67b-d4dfa9b9a0fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "u=5z" :db/id 17592186572525} {:answer/id #uuid "c2fd7900-c51f-5bed-9b31-6871651fb51e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "u=-\frac{1}{5}z" :db/id 17592186572535}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186572535} :answer-field/id #uuid "35a7e094-9492-556b-b055-0b4284ba502d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186572608}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/9e/9e3a9bc6a2c642697cfa2b6525e3abf42a0227f0ac66eecade156a842fb5e92d.png)

The graph above shows a direct variation between the variables $u$ and $z.$ Which equation describes the relationship between the variables?" :question/worked-solution "Since $u$ varies directly with $z,$ we use the equation

$$
u=kz.
$$

Next, we notice there is a point on the graph with $z=-10$ and $u=2.$ So, we substitute this data into the equation to find $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =k\cdot (-10) \\ -\frac{2}{10} & =k \\ -\frac{1}{5} & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
u=-\frac{1}{5}z.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186572723 :question/id #uuid "eabcc9c8-1fae-5b8f-9d65-4f29f12ab5ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-51883" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1746c645-2ca1-5886-a22d-da171cd15a01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "L=50t" :db/id 17592186572342} {:answer/id #uuid "4e190a43-d3de-5ac0-b00b-dc513b13624d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "L=60t" :db/id 17592186572411} {:answer/id #uuid "56acae82-639f-5413-88a9-a7b04e1a0938" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "L=90t" :db/id 17592186572418} {:answer/id #uuid "b3983d19-ed17-57aa-997b-ec527346494e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "L=30t" :db/id 17592186572517} {:answer/id #uuid "ea1c18ae-83f8-5cdc-a1af-f2cbf0066c61" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "L=15t" :db/id 17592186572570}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186572570} :answer-field/id #uuid "bf78e6b5-1138-5983-a5e7-632caf3ecb6f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186572642}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/fa/fa895816cc537fc2ccb30f99f2f9c8ec01cf0ee75ba76fc8a2aed1c0b3349206.png)

$$
L=kt.

$$
\begin{aligned}90 & =k\cdot 6 \\ \frac{90}{6} & =k \\ 15 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the direct variation equation is given by

$$
L=15t.

:topic/math-academy-id 263} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186060460 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060872 :tutorial/content "In isosceles right triangles such as the one shown below, the angles always measure $45^\circ,$ $45^\circ,$ and $90^\circ.$ 

Consequently, isosceles right triangles are often called **$\boldsymbol{45^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{45^\circ}$-$\boldsymbol{90^\circ}$ triangles**.

![](images/d3/d32159528abc75f3ed8bcccaedb2765b676fd6cc64164e2f8c81f98eb37f6db4.png)

All $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles share a special property:

*In any ${45^\circ}$-${45^\circ}$-${90^\circ}$ triangle, the length of the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2}$ times the length of a leg.*

To see why this is, remember that

- in an isosceles triangle, the two legs must have the same length, and

- in a right triangle, the square of the longest side must equal the sum of the squares of the two shorter sides.

So, if an isosceles right triangle has legs of length $a$ and the hypotenuse has length $h,$ then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{2} & ={a}^{2}+{a}^{2} \\ {h}^{2} & =2{a}^{2} \\ h & =\sqrt{2{a}^{2}} \\ h & =\sqrt{2}\cdot a.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "7e5fefd4-4ac4-5999-8c6d-0ad927da9ca6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2381 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8b5ee65a-7747-5a0e-9d06-721118b74e10" :step/math-academy-id 10416 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060461}} {:db/id 17592186060461 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059630 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059462 :question/id #uuid "d1277863-7d33-566d-91b9-7a78458dca8e" :question/math-academy-id "e-3077"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "73ad4cd2-e7f0-5b7d-82fc-1a8e4b0597d8" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060289} {:db/id 17592186060290} {:db/id 17592186497361} {:db/id 17592186497375}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Length of the Hypotenuse of a 45-45-90 Triangle Given the Legs"} :step/id #uuid "0b3e5ddd-300e-5258-b19c-3499c565bdad" :step/math-academy-id 10419 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060462}} {:db/id 17592186060462 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059631 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059463 :question/id #uuid "ce112319-10a9-5483-82c3-566c0630b23a" :question/math-academy-id "e-3080"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d5faa905-dcfc-5eed-b4ed-5818ca6ef342" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048702}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060096} {:db/id 17592186060282} {:db/id 17592186497351} {:db/id 17592186497385} {:db/id 17592186508040}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Length of the Legs of a 45-45-90 Triangle Given the Hypotenuse"} :step/id #uuid "7049be2a-b0af-5170-a1cb-c440a35c6663" :step/math-academy-id 10420 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060473}} {:db/id 17592186060468 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060873 :tutorial/content "Now that we know about $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles, it's straightforward to see that the diagonal of any square is $\sqrt{2}$ times the side length of the square.

To illustrate, consider the square below, where $a$ is the measure of a side and $c$ is the measure of a diagonal.

![](images/07/0743e533eefd4c7e51eaca51c9285fc1b6277553d4f214602a65fc50d1d69ace.png)

Since the sides of a square are congruent, $\triangle{ABC}$ is an isosceles right triangle (a $45^{\circ}$-$45^{\circ}$-$90^{\circ}$ triangle). 

So, for the diagonal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}c=\sqrt{2}\cdot a.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e5c49477-841f-56f9-8779-f1a2a1f115cf" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2382 :tutorial/title "Applications to Squares"} :step/id #uuid "f44a11e0-a932-51d6-97d6-b216a7d42d5f" :step/math-academy-id 10423 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060469}} {:db/id 17592186060469 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059636 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059464 :question/id #uuid "0d244991-c12e-5c56-8f58-762d8be22f8a" :question/math-academy-id "e-3082"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6ae8076e-25bc-5489-ae14-ffa16d17a32c" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060200} {:db/id 17592186060279} {:db/id 17592186497395} {:db/id 17592186497406}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Length of the Diagonal or Side of a Square Given its Perimeter"} :step/id #uuid "247c54c1-1228-55a9-8289-046846fffeeb" :step/math-academy-id 10424} {:db/id 17592186060473 :step/content {:db/id 17592186059638 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186059466 :question/id #uuid "e4466ef9-61d2-5b02-960b-c5c421a9dc1a" :question/math-academy-id "e-3085"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "16fd63e8-664f-53c2-b623-c696b86b5642" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048921}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186060221} {:db/id 17592186060418} {:db/id 17592186497389} {:db/id 17592186497415} {:db/id 17592186508105} {:db/id 17592186508113} {:db/id 17592186562467}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Length of a Hypotenuse or Leg of a 45-45-90 Triangle Given its Perimeter"} :step/id #uuid "718ecaa7-a103-5a7c-a12a-2815eaf19f82" :step/math-academy-id 10430 :step/next {:db/id 17592186060468}}] :activity/title "Isosceles Right Triangles" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186059938} {:db/id 17592186060460 :step/content {:db/id 17592186060872 :tutorial/content "In isosceles right triangles such as the one shown below, the angles always measure $45^\circ,$ $45^\circ,$ and $90^\circ.$

$$

$$
AC=AB\cdot \sqrt{2}=a\sqrt{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+AC \\ 6+3\sqrt{2} & =a+a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 3(2+\sqrt{2}) & =2a+a\sqrt{2} \\ 3(2+\sqrt{2}) & =(2+\sqrt{2})a \\ 3\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})} & =\cancel{(2+\sqrt{2})}a \\ 3 & =a.\end{aligned}
$$

:tutorial/content "When we deal with functions, we are often interested in their largest or smallest values.

- The **global maximum** of a function is the largest $y$-value that the function attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global maximum. It's also called the **absolute maximum.**

- The **global minimum** of a function is the smallest $y$-value that the function attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global minimum. It's also called the **absolute minimum.**

If one or both exist, the global maximum and minimum values of a function are collectively called the **global extrema** of the function. 

For example, in the graph below, the global maximum is $2$, while the global minimum is $-2$.

![](images/22/2235cefbb995edcc085f96d8a5ff4e1ddd83f6345091c90ec3e0a7797fb9d8f3.png)

The point where a function reaches its global maximum/minimum is called the **global maximum/minimum point**.  So in this case, 

- $(-2,2)$ is the global maximum point, and

- $(1,-2)$ is the global minimum point.

**Watch out!** The *global maximum/minimum* is unique. It's a value of the function ($y$-coordinate on the graph). However, there can be several *global maximum/minimum points*. All of these will have the same $y$-coordinate (*global maximum/minimum*) but different $x$-coordinates." :tutorial/id #uuid "cfedbc54-8dd6-532f-9075-109e336b43a6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1495 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a61d8ec6-2820-5303-a832-f51a73657cc2" :step/math-academy-id 3625 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125582}} {:db/id 17592186125582 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124624 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124206 :question/id #uuid "30557b46-f1f0-51dc-94ed-5d84515bc4b0" :question/math-academy-id "e-1112"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "86517de9-0e7c-5c00-a3e8-7aeccbf12d9b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048652}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125072} {:db/id 17592186125176} {:db/id 17592186507446}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Global Maximum of a Function"} :step/id #uuid "ce76583f-0ff9-522f-8324-5c6a6492916a" :step/math-academy-id 3626 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125475}} {:db/id 17592186125583 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124625 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124207 :question/id #uuid "c7c94a49-1a4e-51f6-b0e7-213c67f40fd9" :question/math-academy-id "e-1113"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d9f1c88f-1c8a-52f9-a144-b52f67564f5e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049072}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186125032} {:db/id 17592186125100}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying Whether the Global Extrema of a Function Exist"} :step/id #uuid "a936946d-a2c6-5c5b-8e3e-ad8903a06ff2" :step/math-academy-id 3629}] :activity/title "Global Extrema of Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124693} {:db/id 17592186125581 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125713 :tutorial/content "When we deal with functions, we are often interested in their largest or smallest values.

:step/math-academy-id 16272 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153199}} {:db/id 17592186153196 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153338 :tutorial/content "How does a proportional relationship look when we plot it in the $(x,y)$ plane?

To answer this, let's consider the following proportional relationship:

$$
y = 2x
$$

To plot a graph, we first need a table of values. 

| $x$ | $y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $0$ |  |
| $1$ |  |
| $2$ |  |
| $3$ |  |

Filling in the $y$-values using the equation $y = 2x,$ we get the following:

| $x$ | $y$ |
| --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ |
| $1$ | $2$ |
| $2$ | $4$ |
| $3$ | $6$ |

So, we have the following $(x,y)$ coordinates:

$$
(0,0), \quad (1,2),  \quad (2,4),  \quad (3,6)
$$

If we plot these points in the coordinate plane, we get the following:

![](images/a8/a8cd951c66c67b8f28b791011c7553675b3112029d9ebe4b19769127b5e75bd5.png)

This leads us to the following important fact:

*The graph of any proportional relationship is a straight line that passes through the origin $(0,0)$.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "becbb429-3b12-59c4-8172-aef250c47df9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1507 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1aec00f2-ca4a-5296-be84-e7e83d0f585d" :step/math-academy-id 3709 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152982}} {:db/id 17592186153199 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153339 :tutorial/content "When there is a proportional relationship between $x$ and $y,$ we can express this using the **proportionality symbol** $\propto,$ as follows:

$$
y \propto x
$$

Note that the following statements are all equivalent:

- $y = kx$

- $y$ **varies directly** with $x$

- $y$ is **directly proportional** to $x$

- $y \propto x$" :tutorial/id #uuid "503f0382-0b82-583d-898a-bc1dd1aa02d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1508 :tutorial/title "Alternative Notations and Terminology"} :step/id #uuid "4dc61433-6c56-58c8-9a95-4614aa5f1bf9" :step/math-academy-id 3712 :step/next {:db/id 17592186153200}} {:db/id 17592186153200 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152241 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151799 :question/id #uuid "1a5e8fef-3361-5d24-9abd-d0474a2cd3ae" :question/math-academy-id "e-1141"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5462223e-a206-572a-846a-378621922011" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050613}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152609} {:db/id 17592186152868} {:db/id 17592186498511} {:db/id 17592186498547} {:db/id 17592186520477} {:db/id 17592186572691} {:db/id 17592186572723}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Direct Variation Equation from a Graph"} :step/id #uuid "e8203c67-93c8-55d2-b5fd-7a7003ecaf79" :step/math-academy-id 3715}] :activity/title "Understanding Proportional Relationships Using Graphs" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186152310} {:db/id 17592186153196 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153338 :tutorial/content "How does a proportional relationship look when we plot it in the $(x,y)$ plane?
