$$
f(x)= \sqrt{x-2}
$$

. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(2) &= \sqrt{2 - 2} \\
&= \sqrt{0} \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the graph of $y=f(x)$ "starts" at $x=2$. Let's sketch the graph of $y=f(x)$ as follows:

![](images/a4/a4a64caff7a8b69454ffc8b93a1baad18bf3d93093b3c85a7c4fc3cb9762a2b4.png)

From the graph, we notice that the left-sided limit is

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to 2^-} f(x) = \textrm{DNE}
$$

while the right-sided limit is

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to 2^+} f(x) = 0
$$

Since the two limits are not equal, we conclude that

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to 2} f(x)= \textrm{DNE}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049799} {:db/id 17592186050642} {:db/id 17592186129723 :question/id #uuid "6d3a7b9f-edcc-5a37-bee6-71b22df3defa" :question/math-academy-id "q-3922" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129256 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e3eae4ea-fb38-5efa-843e-783327b82702" :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating the Limit of a Square Root Function"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "b285965a-e603-5a87-ad3a-7ce53eb039a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186127820} {:answer/id #uuid "cb1ba97b-634b-5ab2-924d-cc9550d29b5c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186127821} {:answer/id #uuid "d26cbbb3-365a-5044-b527-135d62972fe3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186127822} {:answer/id #uuid "2f50ff08-d5af-50c7-b86a-03fd63f3058b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186127823} {:answer/id #uuid "496462e6-999a-5292-869e-3d711ab01d07" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "DNE" :db/id 17592186127824}] :answer-field/id #uuid "a75622fa-3456-516d-9426-1ef90c65e3c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186127819}] :question/problem "Calculate $lim_(x → 4^{-})\sqrt{x - 17592186130324 :tutorial/content "Consider the graph of

$$
y=\sqrt{x}
$$

below. We will use this graph to compute $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 4} \sqrt{x} \,$.

![](images/e6/e6423b96ce60348e780ffd437207bdbeb456e3aae2888d7525f8c4e680f4ee43.png)

From the graph, we see that as $x$ approaches $4$, the value of $y$ approaches $\sqrt{4}$. Therefore,

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to 4} \sqrt{x} = \sqrt{4} = 2
$$

The limit of the square root function at a point is equal to the value of the square root function at that point, and this is true for any point *that is greater than $0$.* However, for points that are less than or equal to $0$, the limit does not exist:

$$
lim_(x → c)\sqrt{x} = {\sqrt{c}\begin{vmatrix}ifc > 0 \\ DNE\end{vmatrix}ifc \le 0
$$

Why doesn't the limit exist for

$$
c \leq 0
$$

?

- For $c < 0$, the limit $\lim\limits_{x \to \, c} \sqrt{x}$ does not exist because the square root function $f(x) = \sqrt{x}$ is not defined for negative inputs.
- Although $\sqrt{x}$ is defined at $x=0$, the left limit $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 0^-} \sqrt{x}$ does not exist because $\sqrt{x}$ is undefined left of $x=0$. Consequently, the overall limit $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 0} \sqrt{x}$ does not exist either." :tutorial/id #uuid "065200d4-2dec-598b-bc96-23cbca11d178" :tutorial/math-academy-id 214 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9659c87c-7d2f-5bc9-bfcf-1654a3f32b47" :step/math-academy-id 392 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130190}} {:db/id 17592186130190 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129256 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128928 :question/id #uuid "57abae04-4bc2-5fb4-a5b0-5c0c6c85f955" :question/math-academy-id "e-49"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e3eae4ea-fb38-5efa-843e-783327b82702" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049799} {:db/id 17592186050642} {:db/id 17592186050987}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129723} {:db/id 17592186129818} {:db/id 17592186233586} {:db/id 17592186233766}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating the Limit of a Square Root Function"} :step/id #uuid "b4d1a1fc-a4d5-59ee-a182-8166e3835860" :step/math-academy-id 393 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130193}} {:db/id 17592186130193 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130325 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to our plot of

$$
y=\sqrt x
$$

and work out its limits at infinity.

![](images/a0/a04b7cbc735c20a866b1d22287e2f3a1ffc247931c2de08c545cbd2fe922397b.png)

As $x \to \infty$, the square root function increases without bound. So, we have

$$
\lim_{x\to \infty}\sqrt{x} = \infty
$$

On the other hand, when computing the limit as $x \to -\infty$, remember that the square root function isn't defined for $x<0$. Therefore,

$$
\lim_{x\to -\infty}\sqrt{x} = \textrm{DNE}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "dbe32211-a583-5d8f-a17d-6df81655eadc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 216 :tutorial/title "The Limits at Infinity of the Square Root Function"} :step/id #uuid "51417fe4-26a7-5030-ba58-abf67d0e60d4" :step/math-academy-id 396 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130194}} {:db/id 17592186130194 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129258 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128929 :question/id #uuid "1b850386-4730-512a-8408-932f7b6931b0" :question/math-academy-id "e-50"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ad10ca6b-d130-559b-a201-15127659de13" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050259}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129595} {:db/id 17592186129788} {:db/id 17592186233873} {:db/id 17592186234241} {:db/id 17592186234517}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Limit at Infinity of a Square Root Function"} :step/id #uuid "2dd140f5-c332-59c2-b2fd-408d9ab8c5c6" :step/math-academy-id 397 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130197}} {:db/id 17592186130197 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130326 :tutorial/content "Consider the graph of the cube root function

$$

value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{3}-y$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,2⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2)-f(0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,2⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\ (2(2)^{3}-2)-(2(0)^{3}-1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨6{x}^{2},-1⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨6{c}_{1}^{2},-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =⟨6{c}_{1}^{2},-1⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =12{c}_{1}^{2}-1 \\ 16 & =12{c}_{1}^{2} \\ {c}_{1}^{2} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ {c}_{1} & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}<0<2,$ it's clear that $-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ corresponds to the $x$-coordinate of a point that does not lie on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ Therefore, we can ignore it. Thus, ${c}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}$ to find ${c}_{2}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{2-1} & =\frac{x-0}{2-0} \\ y-1 & =\frac{x}{2} \\ y & =\frac{x}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking into account that ${c}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},$ we obtain that ${c}_{2}=\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+1=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+1.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+1).$"} {:db/id 17592186125015 :question/id #uuid "4e5b6cf6-ccdb-5467-84b0-18bae4498b37" :question/math-academy-id "q-36834"} {:db/id 17592186363052 :question/id $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,2,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,0,-1⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,2,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,0,-1⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,-1)-f(0,2,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,0,-1⟩-⟨0,2,1⟩) \\ 2-(-7) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,-4y,2z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},-4{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =⟨2{c}_{1},-4{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{2}-4{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-2}{(-2)}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ x & =-\frac{y-2}{2}=-\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t,\,\,y=2-2t,\,z=1-2t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t,\,\,{c}_{2}=2-2t,\,{c}_{3}=1-2t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{2}-4{c}_{3}=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t)+8(2-2t)-4(1-2t) & =9 \\ 2t+16-16t-4+8t & =9 \\ -6t & =-3 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =2-2(\frac{1}{2})=1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-2(\frac{1}{2})=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(\frac{1}{2},1,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186363066 :question/id #uuid "3beac47b-9bf4-555f-b72b-5aef346b5fc6" :question/math-academy-id "q-131028"} {:db/id 17592186363073 theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{z}^{3}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨-1,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨0,1,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,1,0)-f(-1,0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨0,1,0⟩-⟨-1,0,1⟩) \\ 0-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,0,-3{z}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},0,-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =⟨2{c}_{1},0,-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =2{c}_{1}+3{c}_{3}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{1}=\frac{z-1}{(-1)} \\ x+1 & =y=1-z\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t-1\,\,y=t,\,z=1-t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t-1\,\,{c}_{2}=t,\,{c}_{3}=1-t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $2{c}_{1}+3{c}_{3}^{2}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t-1)+3(1-t)^{2} & =0 \\ (t-1)[2+3(t-1)] & =0 \\ (t-1)(3t-1) & =0 \\ t & =\frac{1}{3},\,1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem.

- For $t=\frac{1}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}-1=-\frac{2}{3}, \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{1}{3}, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coordinates of the first point $C$ are $(-\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}).$

- For $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =1-1=0, \\ {c}_{2} & =1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-1=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coordinates of the second point $C$ are $(0,1,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186447628 :question/id #uuid "068c9cd0-bc02-5de8-abd9-1e9171a4647c" :question/math-academy-id "q-106255"} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}f(-1,-2,3)-f(0,0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨-1,-2,3⟩-⟨0,0,0⟩) \\ 12-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨-1,-2,3⟩ \\ 12 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨-1,-2,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-1,-1,2z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-1,-1,2{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨-1,-2,3⟩ \\ 12 & =⟨-1,-1,2{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨-1,-2,3⟩ \\ 12 & =1+2+6{c}_{3} \\ 6{c}_{3} & =9 \\ {c}_{3} & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$
x=-t,\,y=-2t,\,z=3t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

$$
{c}_{1}=-t,\,{c}_{2}=-2t,\,{c}_{3}=3t.

$$
\begin{aligned}3t & =\frac{3}{2} \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =-2(\frac{1}{2})=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

can extend the mean value theorem from single-variable calculus to functions of multiple variables.

First, let's recall the mean value theorem from single-variable calculus.

*If $f(x)$ is a function that's continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$, then there exists a point $c\in (a,b)$ such that*

$$
f'(c) = \dfrac {f(b) - f(a)} {b-a}.
$$

Notice that we can rewrite the above equation as follows:

$$
f(b) - f(a) = f'(c) (b-a)
$$

Now, we're ready to present the **multivariable mean value theorem,** which states the following: 

*If $f(x,y)$ is a function that's differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overline{AB},$ then there exists a point $C \in \overline{AB}$ with position vector $\mathbf{c}$ such that 

$$
f(\mathbf{b}) - f(\mathbf{a}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{c}) \cdot (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}),
$$

 where $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are the position vectors of $A$ and $B,$ respectively.*

The theorem naturally extends to functions of three variables.

As an example, let's consider the function 

$$
f(x,y)= x^2 + y^2
$$

 
and the line segment $\overline{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $\mathbf{a} = \langle 1,-1 \rangle$ and $\mathbf{b} = \langle 2,2 \rangle.$ A sketch of this situation is given below.

![](images/67/67c44030beb47bf9cc53a3550da39d3a467fe45445c722803a3a8eaf70f1cb8a.png)

Since $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overline{AB},$ we can apply the mean value theorem. That is, there exists a point $C\in\overline{AB}$ with position vector $\mathbf{c}$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}f(b)-f(a) & =∇f(c)\cdot (b-a) \\ f(2,2)-f(1,-1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,2⟩-⟨1,-1⟩) \\ ({2}^{2}+{2}^{2})-({1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,3⟩ \\ 6 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing out the components of $\nabla f (\mathbf c)$ and expanding the dot product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,3⟩ & =6 \\ ⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c)⟩\cdot ⟨1,3⟩ & =6 \\ {f}_{x}(c)+3{f}_{y}(c) & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the above equation *must* be satisfied by some point $\mathbf c$ that lies on $\overline{AB}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "92fbd1f5-a176-558c-9d91-081244c080f7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5095 segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,2,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,0,-1⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,2,1⟩$ and $b=⟨1,0,-1⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,-1)-f(0,2,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,0,-1⟩-⟨0,2,1⟩) \\ 2-(-7) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,-4y,2z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},-4{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}9 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =⟨2{c}_{1},-4{c}_{2},2{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,-2,-2⟩ \\ 9 & =2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{2}-4{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-2}{(-2)}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ x & =-\frac{y-2}{2}=-\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t,\,\,y=2-2t,\,z=1-2t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t,\,\,{c}_{2}=2-2t,\,{c}_{3}=1-2t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $2{c}_{1}+8{c}_{2}-4{c}_{3}=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t)+8(2-2t)-4(1-2t) & =9 \\ 2t+16-16t-4+8t & =9 \\ -6t & =-3 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =2-2(\frac{1}{2})=1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-2(\frac{1}{2})=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}-x-y$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1,-2,3)-f(0,0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨-1,-2,3⟩-⟨0,0,0⟩) \\ 12-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨-1,-2,3⟩ \\ 12 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨-1,-2,3⟩.\end{aligned}

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-1,-1,2z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-1,-1,2{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
{c}_{1}=-t,\,{c}_{2}=-2t,\,{c}_{3}=3t.

$$
\begin{aligned}3t & =\frac{3}{2} \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =-\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =-2(\frac{1}{2})=-1.\end{aligned}

vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨-1,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨0,1,0⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{z}^{3}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨-1,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨0,1,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,1,0)-f(-1,0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨0,1,0⟩-⟨-1,0,1⟩) \\ 0-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,0,-3{z}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},0,-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =⟨2{c}_{1},0,-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =2{c}_{1}+3{c}_{3}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{1}=\frac{z-1}{(-1)} \\ x+1 & =y=1-z\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t-1\,\,y=t,\,z=1-t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t-1\,\,{c}_{2}=t,\,{c}_{3}=1-t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $2{c}_{1}+3{c}_{3}^{2}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t-1)+3(1-t)^{2} & =0 \\ (t-1)[2+3(t-1)] & =0 \\ (t-1)(3t-1) & =0 \\ t & =\frac{1}{3},\,1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem.

- For $t=\frac{1}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}-1=-\frac{2}{3}, \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{1}{3}, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coordinates of the first point $C$ are $(-\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}).$

- For $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =1-1=0, \\ {c}_{2} & =1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-1=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coordinates of the second point $C$ are $(0,1,0).$"} :step/id #uuid "69751aa3-ae26-5bd3-a4e3-94ae9355433d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485606}} {:db/id 17592186485627 :step/content {:db/id 17592186485572 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b7a5f5b-69d3-59c5-9fe5-d1c3092257a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{2})" :db/id 17592186484837} {:answer/id #uuid "1838f568-f154-5028-8a40-70828f862bea" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,\frac{5}{2})" :db/id 17592186484865} {:answer/id #uuid "31c22ae3-b2f9-5039-88b3-e917ad61579f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{3},\frac{8}{3})" :db/id 17592186484919} {:answer/id #uuid "b3f935b5-6dfe-5bcd-8f1a-c9dd6711bf82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},\frac{5}{2})" :db/id 17592186485207} {:answer/id #uuid "d9857530-796f-58fe-9f92-b5bb11123e5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{3}{5},\frac{11}{5})" :db/id 17592186485274}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186484865} :answer-field/id #uuid "dcf7b736-691e-5d1f-a95e-1aa8428199b5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186485463}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b6c8dce9-3855-5452-ba32-6512e799f65b" :question/math-academy-id "q-36836" :question/problem "Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y)=5{y}^{2}-2x$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,2⟩$ and $b=⟨2,3⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨-2,10y⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨-2,10{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}21 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 21 & =⟨-2,10{c}_{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 21 & =-4+10{c}_{2} \\ 10{c}_{2} & =25 \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-2}{3-2} & =\frac{x-0}{2-0} \\ y-2 & =\frac{x}{2} \\ x & =2y-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{3}-y$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,2⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2)-f(0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,2⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\ (2(2)^{3}-2)-(2(0)^{3}-1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨6{x}^{2},-1⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨6{c}_{1}^{2},-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =⟨6{c}_{1}^{2},-1⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =12{c}_{1}^{2}-1 \\ 16 & =12{c}_{1}^{2} \\ {c}_{1}^{2} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ {c}_{1} & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}<0<2,$ it's clear that $-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ corresponds to the $x$-coordinate of a point that does not lie on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ Therefore, we can ignore it. Thus, ${c}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}$ to find ${c}_{2}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{2-1} & =\frac{x-0}{2-0} \\ y-1 & =\frac{x}{2} \\ y & =\frac{x}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking into account that ${c}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},$ we obtain that ${c}_{2}=\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+1=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+1.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{z}^{3}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨-1,0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨0,1,0⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,1,0)-f(-1,0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨0,1,0⟩-⟨-1,0,1⟩) \\ 0-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨2x,0,-3{z}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨2{c}_{1},0,-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =⟨2{c}_{1},0,-3{c}_{3}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,1,-1⟩ \\ 0 & =2{c}_{1}+3{c}_{3}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-(-1)}{1} & =\frac{y-0}{1}=\frac{z-1}{(-1)} \\ x+1 & =y=1-z\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t-1\,\,y=t,\,z=1-t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t-1\,\,{c}_{2}=t,\,{c}_{3}=1-t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $2{c}_{1}+3{c}_{3}^{2}=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2(t-1)+3(1-t)^{2} & =0 \\ (t-1)[2+3(t-1)] & =0 \\ (t-1)(3t-1) & =0 \\ t & =\frac{1}{3},\,1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we proceed to find the coordinates of the points that satisfy the mean value theorem.

- For $t=\frac{1}{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{3}-1=-\frac{2}{3}, \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{1}{3}, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-\frac{1}{3}=\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coordinates of the first point $C$ are $(-\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}).$

- For $t=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =1-1=0, \\ {c}_{2} & =1, \\ {c}_{3} & =1-1=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coordinates of the second point $C$ are $(0,1,0).$"} :step/id #uuid "69751aa3-ae26-5bd3-a4e3-94ae9355433d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485606}} {:db/id 17592186485606 :step/content {:db/id 17592186485525 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "11ce6875-1f98-55e5-bded-8bc92ce46ff3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{4},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{4})" :db/id 17592186484851} {:answer/id #uuid "386b2c66-1c9c-5668-963d-1846e13ddbee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,-2,3)" :db/id 17592186484936} {:answer/id #uuid "3954fbd2-b037-5d6f-b09b-6ee284cd02dc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,0,0)" :db/id 17592186484938} {:answer/id #uuid "3d60600e-4e34-5bbc-a23b-24df864c14a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{2},-1,\frac{3}{2})" :db/id 17592186484949} {:answer/id #uuid "99ce3a43-46d4-5e6f-9976-ddab31567b2d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{3}{4},-\frac{3}{2},\frac{9}{4})" :db/id 17592186485150}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186484949} :answer-field/id #uuid "90d7f323-818d-52fb-8511-4569536d3e65" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186485427}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "46ec3a18-4fb6-5ee1-a9e8-e76913b4fb34" :question/math-academy-id "q-131031" :question/problem "Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}-x-y$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨-1,-2,3⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

"24eb3f60-8596-5c16-bdd4-fd742e474035" :question/math-academy-id "q-106084" :question/problem "Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y)=2{x}^{3}-y$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,2⟩,$ respectively." :question/worked-solution "The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)=2{x}^{3}-y$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,1⟩$ and $b=⟨2,2⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,2)-f(0,1) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,2⟩-⟨0,1⟩) \\ (2(2)^{3}-2)-(2(0)^{3}-1) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨6{x}^{2},-1⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨6{c}_{1}^{2},-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}15 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =⟨6{c}_{1}^{2},-1⟩\cdot ⟨2,1⟩ \\ 15 & =12{c}_{1}^{2}-1 \\ 16 & =12{c}_{1}^{2} \\ {c}_{1}^{2} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ {c}_{1} & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}<0<2,$ it's clear that $-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$ corresponds to the $x$-coordinate of a point that does not lie on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ Therefore, we can ignore it. Thus, ${c}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}.$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}$ to find ${c}_{2}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-1}{2-1} & =\frac{x-0}{2-0} \\ y-1 & =\frac{x}{2} \\ y & =\frac{x}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & =\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking into account that ${c}_{1}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},$ we obtain that ${c}_{2}=\frac{{c}_{1}}{2}+1=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+1.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}+1).$"} :step/id #uuid "fafd9199-788c-513d-ba61-5620b21205a4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186485598}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c968c8f6-9b7b-5304-a2de-0e2f2c824aa9" :topic/math-academy-id 1101} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097469 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097829 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a vector $\overrightarrow{AB}=\textbf{a}.$ We denote its **magnitude**, also known as its *modulus* or *length*, as $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$ or $|\textbf{a}|.$

For example, the vector below has a magnitude of $8,$ denoted $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=8.$

![](images/71/71105c9d5920ec71e61fe1176021024188a86bd8023671b79e0ce89082994299.png)

Now, let's consider the following situation. Suppose that the vector $\textbf{a}$ is directed vertically upwards and $|\textbf{a}|=6,$ while $\textbf{b}$ is directed horizontally to the right and $|\textbf{b}|=8.$ How can we find $|\textbf{a}+\textbf{b}|?$

First, we use the triangle law of addition to find the resultant $\textbf{a}+\textbf{b}\mathbin{:}$

![](images/ff/ffd155d3b72015a72d878fc8089381a5bcf5a97f698f85945642189ea7368a3f.png)

Notice that we obtain a right triangle. So, we can use the Pythagorean theorem as follows:

$$

:step/content {:db/id 17592186495279 :tutorial/content "A **unit price** is the price of a single item. To compute a unit price, we divide the total cost of a group of items by the number of items in the group.

For example, suppose a store sells a pack of $3$ shirts for $\[math]12.$ 

To find the unit price, we divide the total cost by the number of shirts:

$$
12 \div 3  = 4
$$

Therefore, the unit price is $\[/math]4$ per shirt." :tutorial/id #uuid "1e8ab0cc-4a5e-57ca-a168-f89d110ff113" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3104 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "bd03cc48-369a-5495-aa96-7aa335bd67c7" :step/math-academy-id 616164 :step/next {:db/id 17592186495184}} {:db/id 17592186495249 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495277 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose that installing a fence costs $\[math]360$ per yard. What would be the unit price per foot?

First, notice that there are $3$ feet in $1$ yard.  

To find the unit price per foot, we *divide* the price per yard by $3\mathbin{:}$

$$
360 \div 3 = 120
$$

Therefore, installing the fence costs $\[/math]120$ per foot.

In reverse, if we know that installing a fence costs $\[math]120$ per foot, to find the unit price per yard, we would need to *multiply* the price per foot by $3\mathbin{:}$

$$
120 \times 3 = 360
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "15c0e757-69bb-5bfd-a417-6de7c79fa333" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15094 :tutorial/title "Unit Prices With Units Conversions"} :step/id #uuid "c1f9c4d4-8e93-5221-9ae9-b9e48f28f0d1" :step/math-academy-id 616168 :step/next {:db/id 17592186495214}}] :activity/title "Finding Unit Prices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186494312} {:db/id 17592186495248 :step/content {:db/id 17592186495279 :tutorial/content "A **unit price** is the price of a single item. To compute a unit price, we divide the total cost of a group of items by the number of items in the group.

For example, suppose a store sells a pack of $3$ shirts for $\[math]12.$ 

To find the unit price, we divide the total cost by the number of shirts:

$$
12 \div 3  = 4
$$

Therefore, the unit price is $\[/math]4$ per shirt." :tutorial/id #uuid "1e8ab0cc-4a5e-57ca-a168-f89d110ff113" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3104 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186495277 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose that installing a fence costs $\[math]360$ per yard. What would be the unit price per foot?

First, notice that there are $3$ feet in $1$ yard.  

To find the unit price per foot, we *divide* the price per yard by $3\mathbin{:}$

$$
360 \div 3 = 120
$$

Therefore, installing the fence costs $\[/math]120$ per foot.

In reverse, if we know that installing a fence costs $\[math]120$ per foot, to find the unit price per yard, we would need to *multiply* the price per foot by $3\mathbin{:}$

$$
120 \times 3 = 360
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "15c0e757-69bb-5bfd-a417-6de7c79fa333" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15094 :tutorial/title "Unit Prices With Units Conversions"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046644} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186518269} :activity/id #uuid "3d177d8b-58a3-5a2a-b0d6-cb5cc61ea34f" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186495276 :topic/id #uuid "cef7c109-a883-5959-842c-c3cb8202ae04" :topic/math-academy-id 2555} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186518260 :step/content {:db/id 17592186518207 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "488a6733-2b62-5110-a8a6-e3949dc8cd8b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$$0.09$ per gallon" :db/id 17592186517629} {:answer/id #uuid "4de4fb3c-cdfc-5a86-ac04-dc62c62bcef4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$$16$ per gallon" :db/id 17592186517640} {:answer/id #uuid "4f9e2cfb-824b-5a25-96b9-7b7594c7e4ec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$$24$ per gallon" :db/id 17592186517644} {:answer/id #uuid "65a07d60-9deb-5380-9182-5f188866a085" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$$0.90$ per gallon" :db/id 17592186517675} {:answer/id #uuid "c24e2006-b55b-5eed-b5f2-8ce6d5a28b8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$$28$ per gallon" :db/id 17592186517859}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186517644} :answer-field/id #uuid "be180afd-ef20-5827-b2f6-fd91c64375fd" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186518061}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e1dac973-b461-5ce9-a7ae-b3034ec42db1" :question/math-academy-id "q-354645" :question/problem "Maria bought $1$ cup of olive oil and paid $$1.50$ for it. The symbol "$¬$" represents negation. So, our task is to negate the given sentence. 

To negate our plain English sentence, we place the words "It is not true that" in front of it. This gives the following:

It is not true that $-1$ is greater than $-\sqrt{2}.$

In other words, $-1$ is *not* greater than $-\sqrt{2}.$ Therefore, $¬P$ means the following:

$-1$ is **not** greater than $-\sqrt{2}.$

:topic/math-academy-id 2790} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186152882 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153426 :tutorial/content "The **negation** of a mathematical statement is its *opposite* statement. A mathematical statement and its negation have opposite truth values. 

For example: 

- The negation of the *true* statement "$4$ is divisible by $2$" is the *false* statement "$4$ is **not** divisible by $2.$"

- The negation of the *false* statement "$5$ is even" is the *true* statement "$5$ is odd."

We can express negations using the symbol "$\neg$". The negation of $A$ is denoted $\neg A,$ and has the opposite truth values as $A{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\neg A\,$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |

We can negate compound statements as well. For example, the statement $\neg (A \land B)$ has the opposite truth values as the statement $A \land B{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, A \land B \,$ | $\, \neg (A \land B) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |" :tutorial/id #uuid "65ae07d1-2d1e-5f50-9c5f-4b45ca435aed" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7965 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid have two negations in a row, we can cancel them out.

- For example, $\neg (\neg A)$ can be simplified to $A.$

- Likewise, $\neg (\neg (A \land B))$ can be simplified to $A \land B.$

To understand why negations cancel with each other, consider the following statement: 

$4$ is divisible by $2.$

The negation of this statement is 

$4$ is **not** divisible by $2.$

If we negate again, we get back the original sentence: 

$4$ divisible by $2.$

So, if we negate a statement twice, we end up with the original statement.

More formally, we can prove that $\neg (\neg A) \equiv A$ using a truth table.

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\neg A\,$ | $\,\neg(\neg A)\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |

Since $A$ and $\neg(\neg A)$ have the same truth values, they are logically equivalent." :tutorial/id #uuid "96c8056f-c1d0-5453-ba7f-71700a48506c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7966 :tutorial/title "Double Negations"} :step/id #uuid "42a89cf9-ea00-5196-9579-5a0eda504d5a" :step/math-academy-id 120083 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152887}} {:db/id 17592186152887 :step/content {:db/id 17592186152054 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186151802 :question/id #uuid "503739b1-ea2e-5c6a-8270-6e1fdc050bc4" :question/math-academy-id "e-12683"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "69612c9a-699f-5635-8c9c-649a93ab4583" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186152830} {:db/id 17592186152832} {:db/id 17592186373729} {:db/id 17592186373736} {:db/id 17592186375439} {:db/id 17592186375446} {:db/id 17592186380726} {:db/id 17592186380733} {:db/id 17592186410107} {:db/id 17592186559820} {:db/id 17592186570731} {:db/id 17592186570756} {:db/id 17592186570757}] :knowledge-point/title "Simplifying a Double Negation"} :step/id #uuid "4ca4d75a-1805-5443-b3f6-3a98bafec5cc" :step/math-academy-id 120084}] :activity/title "The "Not" Connective" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186152374} {:db/id 17592186152882 :step/content {:db/id 17592186153426 :tutorial/content "The **negation** of a mathematical statement is its *opposite* statement. A mathematical statement and its negation have opposite truth values. 

For example: 

- The negation of the *true* statement "$4$ is divisible by $2$" is the *false* statement "$4$ is **not** divisible by $2.$"

- The negation of the *false* statement "$5$ is even" is the *true* statement "$5$ is odd."

We can express negations using the symbol "$\neg$". The negation of $A$ is denoted $\neg A,$ and has the opposite truth values as $A{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,\neg A\,$ |
| --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |

We can negate compound statements as well. For example, the statement $\neg (A \land B)$ has the opposite truth values as the statement $A \land B{:}$

| $\,A\,$ | $\,B\,$ | $\, A \land B \,$ | $\, \neg (A \land B) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |" :tutorial/id #uuid "65ae07d1-2d1e-5f50-9c5f-4b45ca435aed" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7965 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d6231d40-48ba-5c9d-855d-04ce17a699e2" :step/math-academy-id 120073 :step/next {:db/id 17592186152883}} {:db/id 17592186153426 :tutorial/content "The **negation** of a mathematical statement is its *opposite* statement. - $P:\pi \text{ is a rational number}$

- $Q:\pi \text{ is a negative number}$" :question/worked-solution "The given sentence is the negation of the following sentence:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(4) & =⟨2-4,\,2\sqrt{4},\,4-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,4,\,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the magnitude of this vector, we obtain

$$

475} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069808 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070009 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have the parametric equations 

$$
x(t) = t+1, \qquad y(t) = t^2+2, \qquad t\in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

These parametric equations trace out a curve in the $xy$-plane. We can combine these into a single function, called a **vector-valued** function $\mathbf r (t),$ as follows:

$$
\mathbf r (t) = \langle x(t), \: y(t)\rangle  =  \langle t+1, \: t^2+2\rangle
$$

The function $\mathbf r (t)$ takes a **parameter** $t$ as input and returns a **position vector**. For a given value of $t,$ each value of $\mathbf{r}(t)$ has its tail at the origin and its terminal point at the coordinates 
$(t+1, \: t^2+2).$

![](images/10/1023d1a1898a402b95d8374f6242d494f714cde9c5ad4cb8186567b9ea192431.png)

Evaluating vector-valued functions is straightforward. Just remember that the output is a vector, not a scalar. 

For the vectors in the graph above, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r(-3) & =⟨(-3)+1,\,(-3)^{2}+2⟩=⟨-2,\,11⟩, \\ r(0) & =⟨(0)+1,\,(0)^{2}+2⟩=⟨1,\,2⟩, \\ r(2) & =⟨(2)+1,\,(2)^{2}+2⟩=⟨3,\,6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5439d77a-b766-5dc3-ad68-6facc632d0f1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7721 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1f95d8fa-a5ab-52bb-954e-880438fde745" :step/math-academy-id 44768 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069809}} {:db/id 17592186069809 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068857 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068457 :question/id #uuid "6eea01b2-bc2a-55a8-9bab-6789df00fc42" :question/math-academy-id "e-12450"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d59ccd52-63db-5d28-b78b-2df7caf52ad0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048293}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069406} {:db/id 17592186069412} {:db/id 17592186259489} {:db/id 17592186319272} {:db/id 17592186319273} {:db/id 17592186345011} {:db/id 17592186345012} {:db/id 17592186345013} {:db/id 17592186387353} {:db/id 17592186393473} {:db/id 17592186427593}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Vector-Valued Function"} :step/id #uuid "4e87da40-1bc7-5937-9854-566b24b722d7" :step/math-academy-id 44769 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069815}} {:db/id 17592186069811 :step/content {:db/id 17592186070010 :tutorial/content "The **magnitude** of a vector-valued function 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left< x(t), \: y(t) \right>,
$$

denoted $|\mathbf{r}(t)|,$ is defined as follows:

$$
|\mathbf{r}(t)| = \sqrt{(x(t))^2+(y(t))^2}
$$

The magnitude of a three-dimensional vector-valued function 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left< x(t), \: y(t), \: z(t) \right>
$$

is defined similarly:

$$
|\mathbf{r}(t)| = \sqrt{(x(t))^2+(y(t))^2+(z(t))^2}
$$

**Note:** An alternative notation that's often used for the magnitude of a vector-valued function is $||\mathbf r(t) ||.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1aaa056f-942b-569d-a4db-4051ddf994ae" :question/worked-solution "Recall that

$$
\int \csc x \cot x \, \textrm dx = - \csc x + C.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-csc⁡xcot⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =-\int (csc⁡xcot⁡x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(-csc⁡x)+C \\  & =csc⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186478558} {:db/id 17592186064562 :question/id #uuid "a5374fc7-a437-5b15-9055-e3e828c62d6f" :question/math-academy-id "q-2042"} {:db/id 17592186064563 :question/id #uuid "25b4ec36-4237-589f-b8e9-2ff52c243e5b" :question/math-academy-id "q-2044"} {:db/id 17592186233194 :question/id #uuid "96dcd1e4-f866-5c31-9249-b3c6a08f3b50" :question/math-academy-id "q-113923"} {:db/id 17592186233195 :question/id #uuid "b17add20-e3fe-557a-b7ba-b30e3097020e" :question/math-academy-id "q-113925" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186064179 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e617f241-254b-5f70-9937-5883b6f28c4f" :knowledge-point/title "Integrating Secant-Tangent and Cosecant-Cotangent"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$\int (2\operatorname{csc}x\,\operatorname{cot}x+\operatorname{sin}x)\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}x\,\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cos}x+C, \\ \int \operatorname{csc}x\operatorname{cot}x\,\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{csc}x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2\operatorname{csc}x\,\operatorname{cot}x+\operatorname{sin}x)\,\text{d}x & =2\int \operatorname{cos}\operatorname{csc}x\,\operatorname{cot}x\,\text{d}x+\int \operatorname{sin}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2(-\operatorname{csc}x)+(-\operatorname{cos}x)+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{csc}x-\operatorname{cos}x+C.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186234311 :question/id #uuid "27d3e02d-3099-56f8-b860-c654c168397f" :question/math-academy-id "q-71657"} {:db/id 17592186250138 :question/id #uuid $$
\int \sec x \tan x \, \textrm dx = \sec x + C.
$$

$$
\eqalign{
		\int (2\sec^2 x + \sec x \tan x )\, \textrm{d}x& = 2 \int \sec^2 x \, \textrm{d}x+ \int \sec x \tan x \, \textrm{d}x \
										&=2\tan x + \sec x + C.

}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186479316} {:db/id 17592186064560 :question/id #uuid "98b12dde-94e6-523e-9264-f15f5987f262" :question/math-academy-id "q-2035"} {:db/id 17592186064849 :question/id #uuid \int \csc^2 x \, \textrm dx = -\cot x + C

\int \csc x \cot x \, \textrm dx = -\csc x + C.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int csc⁡x(csc⁡x+3cot⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡x+3csc⁡xcot⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {csc}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x+3\int csc⁡xcot⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-cot⁡x-3csc⁡x+C.\end{aligned}

$$
\int \cos{x}\,\textrm d x = \sin{x} + C
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cos}x+C \\ \int {sec}^{2}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{tan}x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sec}x\operatorname{tan}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =\operatorname{sec}x+C \\ \int \operatorname{csc}x\operatorname{cot}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{csc}x+C \\ \int {csc}^{2}x\text{ }\text{d}x & =-\operatorname{cot}x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We apply the sum, constant multiple, and power rules as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(u(x) + v(x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} + \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x}
$$

The sum rule also applies to differences:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(u(x) - v(x)) = \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} - \dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x}
$$

As an example, let's calculate the derivative of the function

$$
y = x^2 + x
$$

We can apply the sum rule to find

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}
$$

as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2} + x) \\
&= \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}) + \frac{d}{dx}(x) \\
&= 2x + 1
\end{aligned}

function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown below. How can we plot the graph of $y=f(-x)?$

![](images/51/517dbe715d1f1e79756e6e7bd0d733cc5894f425ac02b2ac1bde2c2a33e86c8d.png)

We can use some points on the graph of $y=f(x)$ to find the corresponding points on the graphs of $y=f(-x).$

For example, let's take the point $(3,4)$. The fact that it's on the graph of $y=f(x)$ means $f(3)=4.$ Then, if $x={\color{red}-3},$ we have

$$
f(-x) = f\left(-({\color{red}-3})\right) = f(3) = 4.
$$

 

This means the point $({\color{red}3},4)$ that lies on $y=f(x)$ has a corresponding point $({\color{red}-3},4)$ that lies on $y=f(-x).$

So, for each point on the graph of $y=f(x),$ there will be a point on the graph of $y=f(-x)$ with the *same* $y$-value and the *opposite* $x$-value:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math]} & \text{Points on [math]y=f(-x)[/math]} \\ (-1,2) & (1,2) \\ (0,-1) & (0,-1) \\ (2,0) & (-2,0) \\ (3,4) & (-3,4)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plot the points and draw the graph of $y = f(-x){:}$

![](images/3a/3ae62ef6496a598d27e485990ab0d3b3cb6f23211de4a015d54614db463bb131.png)

Looking back at the graph, we see that every point on the graph of $y=f(-x)$ is the **reflection across the $y$-axis** of a point on the graph of $y=f(x).$

So, the graph of $y=f(-x)$ can be obtained by reflecting the graph of $y=f(x)$ over the $y$-axis. This result holds in general." :tutorial/id #uuid "333ac18d-4b7d-5c9b-b443-fb3a705515ba" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3283 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "d346ae0a-17ad-5edb-b7f6-751cd8a3e2e7" :step/math-academy-id 18023 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116154}} {:db/id 17592186116154 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115262 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115091 :question/id #uuid "8bbf173b-820a-5b50-b40f-72e4ef09267a" :question/math-academy-id "e-4977"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8ecd0f74-19c3-5770-b376-4d945320f06f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048838}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115496} {:db/id 17592186115524} {:db/id 17592186540091}] :knowledge-point/title "Sketching the Graph of a Horizontally Reflected Function"} :step/id #uuid "d6940736-3c57-5ee2-a4a0-e708da2a4b61" :step/math-academy-id 18028 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116155}} {:db/id 17592186116155 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115263 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115092 :question/id #uuid "5b49540d-4bcd-5ba9-b258-d6ad9828f0e7" :question/math-academy-id "e-4981"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b6912eee-a9ca-5a57-8564-d276afc29711" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115628} {:db/id 17592186115956} {:db/id 17592186540038} {:db/id 17592186540090}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Point that Lies on a Transformed Function"} :step/id #uuid "b05811d8-83b0-566f-8237-c7f9fd933b5f" :step/math-academy-id 18030}] :activity/title "Horizontal Reflections of Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186115419} {:db/id 17592186116153 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116505 :tutorial/content "Consider the function $y=f(x)$ whose graph is shown below. Which of the following could be the equation of the polynomial curve shown above?" :question/worked-solution "First, we notice that the function has precisely three distinct roots, $x=-1$, $x=0$ and $x=2.$

Based on the graph, we can make the following conclusions about the multiplicities of the roots:

- Since the graph is *not* tangent to the $x$-axis at $x=-1,$ this root is a simple root (the multiplicity equals $1$).

The graph of a polynomial $p(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following statements are correct?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $p(x)\to -\infty $ as $x\to \infty .$
- **II.** $x=-1$ is a simple root.
- **III.** $x=2$ is a root of even multiplicity." :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. As $x$ moves right in the positive direction towards $+\infty ,$ the $y$ value moves down in the negative direction towards $-\infty .$

- Statement II is false. The root $x=-1$ is not a simple root because the graph crosses the $x$-axis at the point, and the curve is tangent to the $x$-axis at that point.

- Statement III is false. The root $x=2$ has an odd multiplicity because the graph passes through the $x$-axis at this point.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186326713 :question/id #uuid "fbe22a70-053f-5354-8d7b-dc32dacb2db4" :question/math-academy-id "q-38770"} {:db/id 17592186326715 :question/id roots of a polynomial from its graph. We summarize all possible cases in the table below:

| Multiplicity | Case 1 | Case 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ 

 (Simple root) 

 Odd | ![](images/5a/5a0221f93c65a1eeb4503604a558a6da81c4c7af81c2c52cc35ecf3d189fe99f.png) | ![](images/d5/d556b4edf39181eebb7ec87c344d6f657a6875ecd2745405eaf5351ccaff6f96.png) |
| $>1$ 

 (Multiple root) 

 Even | ![](images/9d/9d14c2588da2ee9c9f5bbc32a70791146bed609ea0d6d5912aeaa2edab02e2d7.png) | ![](images/28/28ad9248a9a509e3a44937d0438fb2366f550a22360d01b9b6a29bcac41357e8.png) |
| $>1$ 

 (Multiple root) 

 Odd | ![](images/3a/3ae81378cb3c918dd5b7730519eb5a91e949f88eef9f03f4910f4ab8fb3cd5a9.png) | ![](images/95/9506a7ce4031f1f6244c0110c3235f66ea5652bb53548a032732869cf21f5997.png) |

Note the following:

- The graph is **tangent** to the $x$-axis at multiple roots. This means that if $x=a$ is a multiple root, then the graph of the polynomial is parallel to the $x$-axis at this point.

- If the multiplicity of a root $x=a$ is *even*, the graph just touches the $x$-axis and reverses direction at $x=a.$

- If the multiplicity of a root $x=a$ is *odd* (including a simple root of multiplicity $1$), the graph crosses the $x$-axis at $x=a.$

- The graph of the polynomial is *never* tangent to the $x$-axis at simple roots." :tutorial/id #uuid "7d750148-b50a-541e-99a4-c4dcd72534bd" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3755 :tutorial/title the fact that the dot product is linear in the first variable, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(5a+3b)\cdot c+(4b+2c)\cdot d & =(5a)\cdot c+(3b)\cdot c+(4b)\cdot d+(2c)\cdot d \\  & =5(a\cdot c)+3(b\cdot c)+4(b\cdot d)+2(c\cdot d).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we can substitute the values for $\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{d},$ and use the fact that the dot product is symmetric to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}5(a\cdot c)+3(b\cdot c)+4(b\cdot d)+2(c\cdot d) & =5(c\cdot a)+3(-1)+4(2)+2(d\cdot c) \\  & =5(c\cdot a)-3+8+2(d\cdot c) \\  & =5(c\cdot a)+5+2(d\cdot c).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting the values for $\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{c},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}5(c\cdot a)+5+2(d\cdot c) & =5(2)+5+2(3) \\  & =10+5+6 \\  & =21.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $(5\mathbf{a}+3\mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{c}+(4\mathbf{b}+2\mathbf{c}) \cdot \mathbf{d} = 21.$"} {:db/id 17592186134199 :question/id #uuid "85c8d44f-ab83-5536-bc23-d67925596d64" $$
\begin{aligned}\alpha \beta (a\cdot b)+12 & =\alpha \beta (b\cdot a)+12.\end{aligned}

$$

#uuid "41c2d289-8df5-551b-9501-3a762c67386f" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About the Dot Product"}] :question/problem "Suppose $(4\mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{a} = {0},$ where $\mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{0}.$ Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{a} = -2(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a})$

II. $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} =  0$

III. $\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 1$" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(4a+2b)\cdot a & =0 \\ (4a)\cdot a+(2b)\cdot a & =0 \\ 4(a\cdot a)+2(b\cdot a) & =0 \\ 2(b\cdot a) & =-4(a\cdot a) \\ b\cdot a & =-2(a\cdot a).\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since $\mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{0},$ we must have $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} > 0.$

- Statement III is false since it leads to a contradiction. Simplifying $(4\mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{a} = {0}$ and substituting in $\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(4a+2b)\cdot a & =0 \\ 4a\cdot a+2b\cdot a & =0 \\ 4a\cdot a+2(1) & =0 \\ a\cdot a & =-\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

but this is a contradiction since $\mathbf{a} \neq \mathbf{0}$ implies that $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} > 0.$

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "I only"."} {:db/id 17592186134198 :question/id #uuid "acd52877-d273-5f8d-88c7-9f3b2d80316c" :question/math-academy-id "q-39197"} {:db/id 17592186134200 :question/id #uuid "94a31460-c755-5749-ae5b-c94244d2f1ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-39204" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133758 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "41c2d289-8df5-551b-9501-3a762c67386f" :knowledge-point/title "Identifying True Statements About the Dot Product"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "ab86b64c-6ab4-51d0-bc53-bc2b9d9020a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I and II only" :db/id 17592186131240} {:answer/id #uuid "c1f4b457-3b5b-540f-b504-d2b1b0be5aaf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186131241} {:answer/id #uuid "22b98eaf-eb11-530a-a4a2-6ee7dc4fced2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186131242} {:answer/id #uuid "2740dcef-96c4-5ed6-b9d3-0d8287a4b5f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "None of the statements are true" :db/id 17592186131243} {:answer/id #uuid "33050ae9-151b-5e50-b859-cb75f312ce42" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499 :db/ident :answer.type/text} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186131244}] :answer-field/id #uuid "ee5bfc63-f8e9-5043-929d-af789ad6720e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186131239}] :question/problem "Suppose $(9a + 3b) \cdot a = 0$, where $a \ne 0$. - **II.** $b\cdot a=a\cdot a$
- **III.** $b\cdot a<0$" :question/worked-solution "Let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since $a\ne 0$, we must have $a\cdot a>0.$

- Statement II is false while statement III is true. Simplifying the expression $(a+b)\cdot a=0$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(a+b)\cdot a & =0 \\ a\cdot a+b\cdot a & =0 \\ b\cdot a & =-a\cdot a\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $a\ne 0$ implies that $a\cdot a>0$, we obtain that $-a\cdot a<0.$

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "III only"."} {:db/id 17592186342140 :question/id #uuid "576bb373-56a3-5da0-ab43-2d02b000f274" :question/math-academy-id "q-74051"} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot 2v & =2(u\cdot v) \\  & =2({u}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}+{u}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}+{u}_{3}\cdot {v}_{3}+{u}_{4}\cdot {v}_{4}) \\  & =2(7\cdot 1+5\cdot 2+(-9)\cdot (-5)+3\cdot (-2)) \\  & =2(7+10+45-6) \\  & =2\cdot 56 \\  & =112.\end{aligned}
$$

To quickly compute the denominator $3\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v},$ we multiply $\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v}$ by $3.$ Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3v\cdot v & =3(v\cdot v) \\  & =3\cdot 34 \\  & =102.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\cdot 2\mathbf{v}}{3\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{v}} =\dfrac{112}{102}=\dfrac{56}{51}.

$$

$$

$$
\frac{u\cdot (2u)}{u\cdot (\frac{1}{3}v)}=\frac{34}{-6}=-\frac{17}{3}.

:topic/math-academy-id 2094} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134623 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135029 :tutorial/content "Recall that for two vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ the **dot product** is defined as the sum of products of corresponding components:

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot v & =\begin{bmatrix}{u}_{1} \\ {u}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {u}_{n}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {v}_{n}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={u}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}+{u}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}+⋯+{u}_{n}\cdot {v}_{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{u}_{i}{v}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e33b6710-6cdf-587d-bba9-185b7686445a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3600 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "580475aa-15f5-5a19-94a0-f3bd4e6576ec" :step/math-academy-id 20179 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134624}} {:db/id 17592186134624 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135030 :tutorial/content "To help us easily carry out computations involving dot products, it is helpful to know some dot product properties. Let $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}$ be any vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ and let $\alpha$ be a scalar in $\mathbb{R}.$ Then, we have the following properties:

- The dot product is **linear in the first variable**, meaning

$$
(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c} \qquad \text{and} \qquad (\alpha \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{b} = \alpha (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}).
$$

- The dot product is **symmetric**, meaning

$$
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{a}.
$$

- The dot product is **positive-definite**, meaning

$$
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} \geq 0,
$$

and $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 0$ if and only if $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0}.$

**Warning**: We cannot compute the dot product of more than two vectors. If we have three vectors $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ then the expression $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c}$ makes no sense. It makes no sense because $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=k$ is a real number, whereas the dot product is only defined for two vectors, so we cannot compute the dot product $k\cdot\mathbf{c}$ of a real number and a vector.

The dot product is also **linear in the second variable**, meaning that

$$
\mathbf{c} \cdot (\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{b} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathbf{a} \cdot (\beta\mathbf{b}) = \beta (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}).
$$

We can prove these two identities using linearity in the first variable and the fact that the dot product is symmetric, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot (a+b) & =(a+b)\cdot c \\  & =a\cdot c+b\cdot c \\  & =c\cdot a+c\cdot b \\ a\cdot (\beta b) & =(\beta b)\cdot a \\  & =\beta (b\cdot a) \\  & =\beta (a\cdot b)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can say that the dot product is linear in both variables." :tutorial/id #uuid "7d6c1e13-da99-5428-8ab9-afc0f1765866" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3601 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Dot {:db/id 17592186135029 :tutorial/content "Recall that for two vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ the **dot product** is defined as the sum of products of corresponding components:

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot v & =\begin{bmatrix}{u}_{1} \\ {u}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {u}_{n}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {v}_{n}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={u}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}+{u}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}+⋯+{u}_{n}\cdot {v}_{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{u}_{i}{v}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e33b6710-6cdf-587d-bba9-185b7686445a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3600 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "580475aa-15f5-5a19-94a0-f3bd4e6576ec" :step/math-academy-id 20179 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134624}} {:db/id 17592186135029 :tutorial/content "Recall that for two vectors $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ the **dot product** is defined as the sum of products of corresponding components:

$$
\begin{aligned}u\cdot v & =\begin{bmatrix}{u}_{1} \\ {u}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {u}_{n}\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}{v}_{1} \\ {v}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {v}_{n}\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={u}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}+{u}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}+⋯+{u}_{n}\cdot {v}_{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{u}_{i}{v}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e33b6710-6cdf-587d-bba9-185b7686445a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3600 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186134624 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135030 :tutorial/content "To help us easily carry out computations involving dot products, it is helpful to know some dot product properties. Let $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}$ be any vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n,$ and let $\alpha$ be a scalar in $\mathbb{R}.$ Then, we have the following properties:

- The dot product is **linear in the first variable**, meaning

$$
(\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{c} \qquad \text{and} \qquad (\alpha \mathbf{a}) \cdot \mathbf{b} = \alpha (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}).
$$

- The dot product is **symmetric**, meaning

$$
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{a}.
$$

- The dot product is **positive-definite**, meaning

$$
\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} \geq 0,
$$

and $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 0$ if and only if $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{0}.$

**Warning**: We cannot compute the dot product of more than two vectors. If we have three vectors $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ then the expression $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{c}$ makes no sense. It makes no sense because $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{b}=k$ is a real number, whereas the dot product is only defined for two vectors, so we cannot compute the dot product $k\cdot\mathbf{c}$ of a real number and a vector.

The dot product is also **linear in the second variable**, meaning that

$$
\mathbf{c} \cdot (\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{b} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathbf{a} \cdot (\beta\mathbf{b}) = \beta (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}).
$$

We can prove these two identities using linearity in the first variable and the fact that the dot product is symmetric, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot (a+b) & =(a+b)\cdot c \\  & =a\cdot c+b\cdot c \\  & =c\cdot a+c\cdot b \\ a\cdot (\beta b) & =(\beta b)\cdot a \\  & =\beta (b\cdot a) \\  & =\beta (a\cdot b)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can say that the dot product is linear in both variables." :tutorial/id #uuid "7d6c1e13-da99-5428-8ab9-afc0f1765866" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3601 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Dot Product"} :step/id #uuid "e6e51146-4580-5c0d-b0e0-ed08d8224588" :step/math-academy-id 20180 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134717}} {:db/id 17592186135030 :tutorial/content "To help us easily carry out computations involving dot products, it is helpful to know some dot product properties. $$

$$

- The dot product is **symmetric**, meaning

$$

- The dot product is **positive-definite**, meaning

The dot product is also **linear in the second variable**, meaning that

$$
\mathbf{c} \cdot (\mathbf{a} + \mathbf{b}) = \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a} + \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{b} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathbf{a} \cdot (\beta\mathbf{b}) = \beta (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}).

$x$ is positive **and** a multiple of $4,$ **or** $x$ is negative.

Express this compound predicate in symbolic form given the following notations:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is positive

- $M(x):$ $x$ is a multiple of $4$

- $N(x):$ $x$ is negative" :question/worked-solution "The word "and" is represented by the symbol "$\land,$" while the word "or" is represented by the symbol "$\lor.$"

Note that this sentence consists of two parts:

- **Part 1:** $x$ is positive and a multiple of $4.$ This corresponds to

$$
\underbrace{x \,\textrm{is positive}}_P \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{and}}_{\land} \quad \underbrace{x \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is a multiple of }4 }_M,
$$

that is, $P \land M.$

- **Part 2:** $x$ is negative. This corresponds to $N.$

So, we can express the sentence as

$$
\underbrace{x \,\textrm{ is positive}\,\textrm{and a multiple of }4 }_{P \land M} \quad \underbrace{\vphantom{p}\textrm{or}}_{\lor} \quad \underbrace{x \vphantom{p}\textrm{ is negative} }_N,
$$

that is, $(P \land M) \lor N.$"} {:db/id 17592186198691 :question/id #uuid "65e7d617-d603-5bc0-8425-500e7ed05a4a" :question/math-academy-id "q-170741"} {:db/id 17592186198692 :question/id #uuid "e6d7fc87-c9d5-5ec1-9313-97840cdea5be" :question/math-academy-id "q-170743" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198253 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ce659c55-ca26-52c6-b15e-ec317013d856" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Nested Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a506dcfe-4cec-5d6a-92b6-e01253a0c863" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(O∧E)∧(N∧P)" :db/id 17592186194779} {:answer/id #uuid "ce08a6b9-09b8-5a85-9e1f-70b6689cbee1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(O∨E)∧(N∨P)" :db/id 17592186194780} {:answer/id #uuid "fe0ba6e6-ac14-5c01-ab04-354cad316027" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "(O∨E)∨(N∨P)" :db/id 17592186194781} {:answer/id #uuid "409e2007-9a38-5696-9da9-eaeaf9f1209d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "((O∧E)∧N)∧P" :db/id 17592186194782} {:answer/id #uuid "6f748e69-8c13-524b-bfe8-82199f40cd15" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "((O∨E)∧N)∨P" :db/id 17592186194783}] :answer-field/id #uuid "f941fb41-1019-5d5f-b49a-6f151680cdc1" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186194778}] :question/problem "> $x$ is odd **or** even, **and** $x$ is negative **or** positive.

#uuid "e6bc626a-9517-584c-bf55-8653227f830e" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Truth Sets of Conjunctions and Disjunctions"}] :question/problem "Find the truth set of $P(x) \lor Q(x)$ given the following predicates defined over the universal set $\mathbb{R}{:}$

- $P(x):$ $3x -1 < 5$

- $Q(x):$ $x \geq 3$" :question/worked-solution "The truth set of $P(x) \lor Q(x)$ represents the *union* of the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x){:}$

$$
T_{P \lor Q} = T_P \cup T_Q
$$

We start by finding the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x){:}$

- To find the the truth set of $P(x),$ we solve the following inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-1 & <5 \\ 3x & <6 \\ x & <2\end{aligned}
$$

 
So, the truth set of $P(x)$ is
$T_P = (-\infty,2).$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 
$T_Q = [3,\infty).$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P∨Q} & ={T}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\  & =(-\infty ,2)\cup [3,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198704 :question/id #uuid "67540ebf-2612-5ae3-8a6d-03d5320b1acb" :question/math-academy-id "q-171558"} {:db/id 17592186198705 :question/id #uuid 17592186199039 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199520 :tutorial/content "We can apply the logical operations of conjunction and disjunction to predicates.

- The **conjunction** of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is a new predicate which we denote as follows: 

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \land Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)
$$

This conjunction is true whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true *and* $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is true for a specific set of respective variable assignments. The conjunction is false if either $P$ or $Q$ is false.

- The **disjunction** of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is written as follows:

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \lor Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)
$$

This disjunction is true whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true, $Q(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_m)$ is true, or both are true, for a specific set of variable assignments. The disjunction is false if $P$ *and* $Q$ are false.

For example, consider the following predicates:

- $P(n):$ $n$ is even

- $Q(n):$ $n$ is positive

Then, $P(n) \land Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *and* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even and positive."

On the other hand, $P(n) \lor Q(n)$ is a new predicate that reads "$n$ is even *or* $n$ is positive," which can be simplified to "$n$ is even or positive."

When it's clear that $P(n)$ is a predicate in the variable $n,$ we sometimes omit the variables when writing them. So, $P(n) \land Q(n)$ and $P(n) \lor Q(n)$ can be written as $P \land Q$ and $P \lor Q,$ respectively." :tutorial/id #uuid "c05b0e9a-b514-5c42-9d07-7ec2466b30be" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7984 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b041ca76-9538-556f-ba42-756566d8edf6" :step/math-academy-id 120115 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199040}} {:db/id 17592186199040 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198252 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198099 :question/id #uuid "d40cb0df-fce7-5236-b0ef-62f5a343b3a3" :question/math-academy-id "e-12724"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2993b4ab-e45b-579a-8a11-b5e9ee107d5b" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048778}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198689} {:db/id 17592186198690} {:db/id 17592186381368} {:db/id 17592186381495} {:db/id 17592186389656}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form"} :step/id #uuid "8701928d-1944-5363-b962-b4891f892daa" :step/math-academy-id 120116 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199041}} {:db/id 17592186199041 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198253 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198100 :question/id #uuid "3e2319b4-ab10-50ef-845b-9586c9761227" :question/math-academy-id "e-12725"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ce659c55-ca26-52c6-b15e-ec317013d856" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198691} {:db/id 17592186198692} {:db/id 17592186381375} {:db/id 17592186381382} {:db/id 17592186381502} {:db/id 17592186389670} {:db/id 17592186389710} {:db/id 17592186426839}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Nested Compound Predicate in Symbolic Form"} :step/id #uuid "77ba67c1-cc43-57be-ac98-62a769bb7e42" :step/math-academy-id 120119 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199042}} {:db/id 17592186199042 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199521 :tutorial/content "Let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

From the definition of the conjunction of predicates, we have that $P \land Q$ is true if both $P$ and $Q$ are true. Therefore, the truth set of $P \land Q$ is the *intersection* of the truth sets of $P$ and $Q{:}$

$$
T_{P \land Q} = T_P \cap T_Q
$$

For example, consider the following predicates defined over the set of positive integers:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is divisible by $3$

- $Q(x):$ $24$ is divisible by $x$

We start by finding the truth sets of $P(x)$ and $Q(x){:}$

- The truth set of $P(x)$ is 

$$
T_P = \big\{ 3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27 \ldots \big\}.
$$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 

$$
T_Q = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24 \big\}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P∧Q} & ={T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q} \\  & =\{3,6,9,12,15,18,21,24,27…\}\cap \{1,2,3,4,6,8,12,24\} \\  & =\{3,6,12,24\}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "74eb89b1-6654-56b5-9fef-718a3acfcb2f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7985 :tutorial/title "The Truth Set of a Conjunction"} :step/id #uuid "ea6a5438-89a7-508e-92fb-e311fd2c5c48" :step/math-academy-id 120122 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199043}} {:db/id 17592186199043 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199542 :tutorial/content "Once again, let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. 

From the definition of the disjunction of predicates, we have that $P \lor Q$ is true if $P$ is true, or $Q$ is true, or both are true. Therefore, the truth set of $P \lor Q$ must be the *union* of the truth sets of $P$ and $Q{:}$

$$
T_{P \lor Q} = T_P \cup T_Q
$$

For example, suppose we are given the following shaded regions that represent the truth sets of the predicates $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y),$ defined over the universal set $\mathbb{R}^2.$ 

![](images/ce/ce71e62503acd1c82f6bba7e1d9c83c40f0a98f04c689c3ccd58e7a99a814856.png)

To get the truth set of $P(x,y) \lor Q(x,y),$ we take all the points that belong to $T_P$ or $T_Q,$ as shown below.

![](images/9c/9c528c5fe390bd1f22cb473c01b768e83f5b3a35d97eb7e670c6734b8cb2c2f8.png)

**Note:** The points where the *dashed* line meets the *solid* curve belong to $T_P \cup T_Q$ since these points lie in $T_P.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "4d1b797a-ff89-514d-a0df-87d6858b45e3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8140 :tutorial/title "The Truth Set of a Disjunction"} :step/id #uuid "9905e635-bc99-5ab6-8557-95a009250e4e" :step/math-academy-id 120123 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199044}} {:db/id 17592186199044 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198254 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198101 :question/id #uuid "3a115dd5-3241-5627-bb40-121b75eeb7ae" :question/math-academy-id "e-12726"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e6bc626a-9517-584c-bf55-8653227f830e" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048592}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198704} {:db/id 17592186198705} {:db/id 17592186381410} {:db/id 17592186381551} {:db/id 17592186381579} {:db/id 17592186389783} {:db/id 17592186389790} {:db/id 17592186426840}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Truth Sets of Conjunctions and Disjunctions"} :step/id #uuid "69f763bb-fe3d-5367-b28c-7de5d1163729" :step/math-academy-id 120124 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199045}} {:db/id 17592186199045 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199523 :tutorial/content "Conjunction and disjunction of predicates are generalizations of logical operations on statements. Moreover, the properties of these operations on statements can be translated to corresponding operations on predicates. 

In particular, the idempotent, absorption, associative, and commutative laws also apply to conjunction and disjunction of predicates. 

So, for predicates $P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n),$ $Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),$ and $R(z_1,z_2\ldots,z_p),$ we have the following:

- *The Idempotent Laws*: 

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧P≡P∨P≡P\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Associative Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧(Q∧R) & ≡(P∧Q)∧R \\ P∨(Q∨R) & ≡(P∨Q)∨R\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Commutative Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧Q & ≡Q∧P \\ P∨Q & ≡Q∨P\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Distributive Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧(Q∨R) & ≡(P∧Q)∨(P∧R) \\ P∨(Q∧R) & ≡(P∨Q)∧(P∨R)\end{aligned}
$$

- *The Absorption Laws*:

$$
\begin{aligned}P∧(P∨Q) & ≡P \\ P∨(P∧Q) & ≡P\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6ad96982-4e36-52f9-816a-db64ba277433" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7989 :tutorial/title "Laws Involving Conjunction and Disjunction of Predicates"} :step/id #uuid "71a8a715-2397-5052-a148-b7cc79853a2b" :step/math-academy-id 120128 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199046}} {:db/id 17592186199046 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198255 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198104 :question/id #uuid "2ab89571-f4e2-515f-9d01-b1213e73ffc0" :question/math-academy-id "e-12733"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5f674fcf-7f3e-53c0-8759-6f83b0820160" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049824}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198697} {:db/id 17592186198698} {:db/id 17592186381389} {:db/id 17592186381396} {:db/id 17592186381403} {:db/id 17592186401674} {:db/id 17592186401681} {:db/id 17592186426838} {:db/id 17592186426841} {:db/id 17592186516871}] :knowledge-point/title "Using Laws Involving Conjunction and Disjunction"} :step/id #uuid "1887f6f2-227f-5082-89ee-2e84c56eb994" :step/math-academy-id 120129}] :activity/title "The "And" and "Or" Connectives With Predicates" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198514} {:db/id 17592186199039 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199520 :tutorial/content "We can apply the logical operations of conjunction and disjunction to predicates.
